# What Happens When You Die? What the Bible Really Teaches

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/what-happens-when-you-die-bible/
Category: Bible Answers
Author: Daniel Moore
Published: 2026-10-25

A gentle look at death, the resurrection, and the hope of seeing our loved ones again.


The phone call came late at night. Or maybe it was a slow goodbye in a hospital room, holding a hand that grew quieter and then finally still. If you have lost someone you love, you know the questions that come afterward, often in the middle of the night. Where are they now? Can they see me? Are they at peace? Will I ever hold them again?

At the start of November, many families feel these questions even more deeply. Toussaint and the days around it bring candles, cemetery visits, flowers on graves, and memories of mothers, fathers, grandparents, and children who are gone. For many Haitian families, it is a season when the line between the living and the dead can feel especially thin.

The Bible does not leave us guessing about any of this. It speaks about death honestly, without pretending it is anything less than an enemy. And it speaks about hope even more boldly, with promises that reach all the way to resurrection morning. In this article we will look carefully at what Scripture actually teaches, answer the passages people most often ask about, and see why this teaching brings so much comfort to grieving hearts.

## The short answer

- Sleep : How Jesus described death (John 11:11)
- No time : Passes for those who rest in Jesus
- One morning : When the dead in Christ rise together

The Bible teaches that when a person dies, they rest unconscious in the grave, much like a deep and dreamless sleep, until Jesus returns and raises them to life. The faithful do not drift as spirits, wander between worlds, or watch from somewhere unseen. Their next conscious moment will be hearing the voice of Jesus calling them home at the resurrection (John 5:28 to 29, 1 Thessalonians 4:16).

This is the official teaching of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, set out in Fundamental Belief 26 on death and resurrection, and it rests on a consistent reading of Scripture from Genesis to Revelation rather than on one or two verses. Christians from several traditions have held this understanding throughout history. Let us walk through why, starting at the very beginning.

- Life : God gives the breath of life
- Death : The body rests in the grave
- Waiting : No awareness of time passing
- His return : Jesus comes with a shout
- Resurrection : Raised to live forever

## How God made us helps explain death

To understand what happens at death, it helps to start with how God created life in the first place. The Creation story gives us a simple and beautiful picture of what a human being is.

> "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Genesis 2:7, KJV

Notice the formula in this verse. God took dust from the ground, added the breath of life, and the result was a living soul. Adam did not receive a soul as a separate part that was placed inside his body. He became a soul. Throughout the Old Testament, the word "soul" usually means the whole living person, which is why Scripture can speak of a certain number of "souls" traveling with Jacob to Egypt, meaning people.

**The Creation formula**
- Dust of the ground (the body)
- Plus the breath of life from God
- Equals a living soul, the whole person (Genesis 2:7)
- At death the formula reverses: dust returns to the earth and the breath returns to God (Ecclesiastes 12:7)

Death simply reverses what happened at Creation. "Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it" (Ecclesiastes 12:7). The Hebrew word for spirit in this verse, ruach, also means breath or wind. Job uses it the same way when he says "the spirit of God is in my nostrils" (Job 27:3), clearly speaking about his breath.

So at death, the body returns to the dust, and the breath of life that God gave returns to Him. What returns to God is not a conscious ghost carrying the person's thoughts, but the life force He loaned. The person rests, and God holds every detail of who they were safely in His care until the day He gives them life again.

## What the Bible says about the dead

When we read the passages that speak directly about the condition of the dead, a clear and consistent picture appears. These verses come from different writers across many centuries, yet they say the same thing in plain language.

| Popular idea | What Scripture teaches |
| --- | --- |
| The dead watch over us | The dead know nothing and have no part in life on earth (Ecclesiastes 9:5 to 6) |
| The soul is naturally immortal | God alone has immortality and gives it at the resurrection (1 Timothy 6:16, 1 Corinthians 15:53) |
| The faithful are already in heaven | Even David has not ascended into the heavens (Acts 2:34) |
| Spirits of the dead visit the living | The dead rest in silence until Jesus calls them (Psalm 115:17, John 5:28 to 29) |
| Death is the end of hope | The dead in Christ will rise first when He returns (1 Thessalonians 4:16) |

Ecclesiastes states it most directly: "For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing" (Ecclesiastes 9:5). The writer goes on to say that the dead no longer have any part in anything that happens "under the sun" (Ecclesiastes 9:6). Their love, their worries, and their plans have all come to rest. They are not watching events unfold on earth or carrying the weight of what happens to the family they left behind.

The Psalms describe the same reality. "His breath goeth forth, he returneth to his earth; in that very day his thoughts perish" (Psalm 146:4). Another psalm says, "The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence" (Psalm 115:17). If the faithful went straight to heaven at death, we would expect the psalmist to describe them praising God more fully than ever. Instead, he describes the grave as a place of silence and rest.

The New Testament adds an important truth about immortality. Paul writes that God "only hath immortality" (1 Timothy 6:16). In other words, human beings are not naturally immortal. Immortality is a gift that God gives to the redeemed at the resurrection, when "this mortal must put on immortality" (1 Corinthians 15:53). It is not something we carry inside us by nature.

Even the greatest heroes of faith are still waiting for that day. King David, called a man after God's own heart (1 Samuel 13:14), died about a thousand years before Christ. Yet on the day of Pentecost, Peter told the crowd in Jerusalem, "David is not ascended into the heavens" (Acts 2:34). David's tomb was still with them, and David himself was resting until the resurrection.

## Jesus called death a sleep

Perhaps the clearest teaching about death comes from Jesus Himself. When His dear friend Lazarus died, Jesus told His disciples, "Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep" (John 11:11). The disciples misunderstood and thought Lazarus was simply resting from illness, so Jesus told them plainly, "Lazarus is dead" (John 11:14).

That was the picture Jesus chose to describe death, and He chose it carefully. Sleep is real, and it involves no awareness of passing time. But sleep is not the end. You lie down at night expecting to wake up in the morning. For those who belong to Jesus, death is a sleep that will end with the brightest morning the world has ever seen.

What is striking about the story of Lazarus is what Lazarus did not say. He lay in the tomb for four days, long enough that his sisters worried about the smell. If he had been in heaven during those days, he would have had the greatest story ever told, and surely someone would have written it down. Yet Scripture records no report from him about the afterlife, because there was nothing to report. He was asleep until Jesus called his name.

The rest of the New Testament uses this same language again and again. When Stephen became the first Christian martyr, Luke writes that "he fell asleep" (Acts 7:60). Paul comforts believers about loved ones "which are asleep" (1 Thessalonians 4:13). And centuries earlier, the prophet Daniel described the dead as those who "sleep in the dust of the earth" and who "shall awake" (Daniel 12:2). The Bible speaks with one voice on this.

## The great hope: resurrection morning

If death were the whole story, this would be a very sad article. It is not. The Bible's answer to death is not a shadowy, ghostly afterlife. It is a resurrection, with a real body, a real reunion with the people we love, and a real face to face meeting with Jesus.

> "For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air." 1 Thessalonians 4:16 to 17, KJV

Read those words slowly, especially the phrase "together with them." Paul wrote this letter to believers who were grieving the loss of loved ones, so that they would "sorrow not, even as others which have no hope" (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Christians still grieve, and our tears are real. But we grieve with a reunion in view, the way you might cry at an airport while already looking forward to the day you will be together again.

- At death: Rest in the grave: The believer falls asleep in Jesus, unaware of passing time (Ecclesiastes 9:5).

- The second coming: The first resurrection: Jesus returns with a shout and the dead in Christ rise first (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

- The same moment: Changed and caught up: Living believers are changed in the twinkling of an eye and meet the Lord together with them (1 Corinthians 15:52).

- The thousand years: Reigning with Christ: The redeemed live and reign with Christ, while the rest of the dead wait (Revelation 20:4 to 5).

- Forever: No more death: God wipes away every tear, and death itself is gone (Revelation 21:4).

Paul describes the moment of resurrection in 1 Corinthians 15. "In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump... the dead shall be raised incorruptible" (verse 52). Our weak and mortal bodies will "put on immortality" (verse 53), and the whole church will sing a song of victory: "O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?" (verse 55). Death, which has taken so much from so many, will finally lose.

Jesus made this promise personal when He stood outside the tomb of Lazarus. "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live" (John 11:25). That same hope carried believers long before Jesus came. Job, in the middle of terrible suffering, declared, "I know that my redeemer liveth," and looked forward to seeing God "in my flesh" (Job 19:25 to 26). The hope of the resurrection runs through the whole Bible.

## Why this teaching brings comfort

Some people worry at first that the idea of death as a sleep sounds cold or sad. In practice, many grieving families find it deeply freeing, once they understand what it means for the people they love.

**Three comforts for grieving hearts**
- Your loved one is not suffering or waiting anxiously
- Your loved one is not watching your pain
- You never need to fear the dead, because they rest in God's care

First, it means your loved one is not suffering or waiting anxiously somewhere. For the person who dies trusting in Jesus, no time passes at all. They close their eyes in death, and their very next awareness will be resurrection morning, seeing Jesus coming in glory. This is why Paul could say he wanted to "depart, and to be with Christ" (Philippians 1:23). From the believer's point of view, death is followed immediately by Christ's appearing, even if centuries pass on earth.

Second, it means your loved one is not watching your pain. Many people imagine a mother in heaven seeing her children struggle, or a grandfather watching the family argue and drift apart. If that were true, heaven would be a place of constant heartbreak. The Bible spares the dead that grief. They rest in peace, untouched by sorrow, until the day God wipes away every tear from every eye (Revelation 21:4).

Third, it means you do not need to fear the dead. They cannot harm you, haunt you, punish you, or demand anything from you. They are not angry spirits that must be calmed or pleased. They are safe in God's memory, and nothing about who they were is lost to Him. When the resurrection comes, God will restore them fully.

## A word to Haitian families

Many of us grew up in homes where the dead never felt far away. We heard that spirits visit in dreams, that they need to be fed or honored, or that they can bring blessing or trouble to the living depending on how they are treated. Around Fèt Gede in early November, these beliefs become especially visible across Haiti and throughout the diaspora, from Port au Prince to Miami to here in Texas.

These traditions often grow out of real love for those who have died and a deep longing to stay connected to them. That longing is not wrong. It is a sign of how much our families matter to us, and God Himself placed that love in our hearts. He understands it better than anyone.

But Scripture gives a clear and loving warning. God told Israel not to consult mediums or anyone who seeks to speak with the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10 to 12). The prophet Isaiah asks a searching question: "should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?" (Isaiah 8:19). Since the Bible teaches that the dead know nothing, any voice, dream, or presence that claims to be a departed loved one cannot truly be them. The Bible warns that spiritual deception is real, and that the enemy can even disguise himself as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14).

The good news here is freedom. You do not owe the dead anything, and you do not have to keep them happy or protect yourself from them. Jesus says He holds "the keys of hell and of death" (Revelation 1:18), which means no power in the spirit world has the final word over your family. Your loved ones who trusted Him are in His hands, and so are you. You can honor their memory with gratitude, stories, and love, while placing your trust fully in the living God.

## Questions people ask

Whenever this topic is discussed, a few passages are often raised as evidence that the dead are conscious. These are sincere questions that deserve careful answers. Here is how Adventists understand each one in the light of the whole Bible.

### What about the thief on the cross?

In Luke 23:43, Jesus says to the repentant thief, "Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." The original Greek manuscripts had no punctuation, so translators must decide where to place the comma. The verse can be read as, "I say unto thee today, you will be with me in paradise," an emphatic promise given on the darkest day of Jesus' life. This reading fits the rest of Scripture well. On Sunday morning, after His resurrection, Jesus told Mary, "I am not yet ascended to my Father" (John 20:17). Jesus Himself did not go to paradise that Friday, so the thief could not have joined Him there that day. The promise was certain, and its fulfillment comes at the resurrection.

### Doesn't Paul say to be absent from the body is to be present with the Lord?

In 2 Corinthians 5:8, Paul expresses his longing to be with Christ. But the verses just before (2 Corinthians 5:1 to 4) explain what he is longing for. He describes groaning to be "clothed upon" with a new, heavenly body, not to be "unclothed" as a bodiless spirit. Elsewhere Paul is clear that his reward will come "at that day," when Jesus appears (2 Timothy 4:8). Because no time passes for those who rest in death, the believer who dies moves, from their own point of view, directly into the presence of the Lord at His coming.

### What about the rich man and Lazarus?

Luke 16:19 to 31 is a parable, part of a series of stories Jesus told in Luke 15 and 16 to teach spiritual lessons. If we read it literally, it would mean that heaven and hell are close enough for people to talk across, and that a drop of water on the tongue could ease a soul in flames. Jesus used a story familiar to His listeners to make one central point: our choices in this life matter eternally, and Scripture is enough to lead us to repentance (Luke 16:31). The parable was never meant to be a map of the afterlife.

### Can our loved ones see us from heaven?

According to Ecclesiastes 9:5 to 6, the dead know nothing and have no part in what happens on earth. That may feel hard to hear at first, especially if you have found comfort in imagining a loved one watching over you. But it means they are spared the sorrow of watching us suffer, struggle, or grieve. They are resting in peace, and the joy of seeing one another again is waiting for resurrection day, when it will be complete and never end.

Related: [Does Hell Burn Forever? What the Bible Really Says About Hell](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/does-hell-burn-forever-what-the-bible-says/)

## Reflection questions

Take some quiet time with these questions, perhaps with your Bible open beside you. Begin by asking which promise about the resurrection speaks most to your heart right now, and why it matters so much to you. Then consider how knowing that your loved one is resting, not watching, might change the way you carry your grief. Finally, ask God honestly whether there is any fear about death or the dead that He wants to lift from you today.

## A word of encouragement

If you are grieving, your tears are not a sign of weak faith. Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus, even though He knew He would raise him to life just minutes later (John 11:35). He was moved by the sorrow of the people around Him, and He is moved by yours too. You never grieve alone.

And remember this: Jesus has already walked out of His own tomb. Because He lives, death is not the last word for anyone who trusts Him. One day very soon the graves will open, families will be reunited, mothers will hold their children again, and death itself will be gone forever. Until that morning, you can rest in His promise and lean on His people.

## A prayer

Jesus, You know what it feels like to lose someone You love, because You wept at the grave of Your friend. Thank You for being the resurrection and the life. Hold every heart that is grieving today, and draw near to those who feel alone in their sorrow. Free us from fear of death and of the dead, and fill us with hope for the morning when You will call our loved ones by name. Until that day, keep us close to You. Amen.

## Your next step

If you are carrying grief right now, you do not have to carry it alone. Our church family would be honored to pray with you, and you can share a request through our prayer request page, either with your name or anonymously. If you would like to explore what the Bible says about death, the resurrection, and the second coming of Jesus at your own pace, you can also request a free Bible study below with someone from Shekinah who would be glad to walk alongside you.

- Source: [What We Believe: The 28 Fundamental Beliefs, Adventist.org](https://www.adventist.org/beliefs/)

# Why Do Seventh-day Adventists Worship on Saturday?

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/why-do-seventh-day-adventists-worship-on-saturday/
Category: Bible Answers
Author: Jack Thompson
Published: 2026-10-25

The Bible story, the history, and the heart behind Sabbath worship, plus honest answers to the questions people ask most.


Maybe a coworker turned down your Saturday barbecue because she had church that morning. Maybe you drove past a full parking lot on a Saturday and wondered what was going on inside. Or maybe you grew up keeping Sunday, and one day someone handed you a Bible verse that left you more curious than you expected. Questions like these are how many people first meet Seventh-day Adventists, and they are good questions to ask.

Whatever brought you here, it deserves more than a one line answer. Seventh-day Adventists worship on Saturday because the Bible names the seventh day as the Sabbath that God blessed at Creation, wrote into the Ten Commandments, and that Jesus Himself kept. For Adventists, this is not a rule for earning salvation or a badge of being better than other Christians. It is a weekly appointment with the God who has already saved them, a standing invitation to stop, rest, and remember who they belong to.

In this article we will walk slowly through what Scripture says from Genesis to Revelation, look honestly at how Sunday worship became common in church history, answer the passages people most often raise, and paint a picture of what the Sabbath actually looks like in a real home. You do not have to agree with everything here to find it helpful. Our hope is simply that you will open your own Bible, read the passages for yourself, and let God speak.

## The short answer

- 7th : The day God blessed and made holy at Creation
- 24 hours : Sunset Friday to sunset Saturday
- 4th : Commandment of the Ten that names the day

Adventists keep Saturday as the Sabbath because the Bible consistently calls the seventh day holy, and nowhere in Scripture does God move that blessing to another day. From the first chapter of Genesis to the prophecies of the new earth, the seventh day stands out as a day God made, blessed, and set apart for Himself and for His people.

The Sabbath runs from Friday at sunset to Saturday at sunset. That may sound unusual today, but it follows the biblical way of counting days from evening to evening. In the Creation story each day is described as "the evening and the morning" (Genesis 1:5), God later told Israel to keep holy time "from even unto even" (Leviticus 23:32), and the Gospels show people waiting until the sun had set on the Sabbath before bringing their sick to Jesus (Mark 1:32). So when the sun goes down on Friday, holy time begins.

That conviction rests on five threads that run through the whole Bible. Each one strengthens the others, and together they form the reason Adventists gather for worship on the seventh day.

**The five threads at a glance**
- Creation: God blessed the seventh day before sin or any nation existed (Genesis 2:2 to 3)
- Commandment: the fourth of the Ten Commandments names the seventh day (Exodus 20:8 to 11)
- Christ: Jesus kept the Sabbath and called Himself its Lord (Luke 4:16, Mark 2:28)
- Church: the apostles kept worshiping on the Sabbath after the resurrection (Acts 13, 16, 17, 18)
- Covenant: the Sabbath is a sign of freedom and belonging to God (Ezekiel 20:20)

## 1. The Sabbath began at Creation, before there were any Jews

The Sabbath is older than Israel, older than Moses, and older than sin itself. It did not begin at Mount Sinai or in a synagogue. It began in the Garden of Eden, in a perfect world, as the final touch on God's work of Creation.

> "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made. And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it." Genesis 2:2 to 3, KJV

Notice that God did three things to that day. He rested on it, He blessed it, and He sanctified it, which means He set it apart for holy use. He did not do these things to any other day of the week. God was not tired, so His rest was not about exhaustion. It was about delight in what He had made and about creating space for relationship with the people He had just formed in His image.

This matters because many sincere Christians assume the Sabbath was given only to the Jewish nation. Yet Jesus said plainly, "The sabbath was made for man" (Mark 2:27). The word He used points to humanity as a whole, not to one ethnic group. Adam and Eve were not Jewish. Abraham would not be born for many generations. The Sabbath was a gift to the entire human family, woven into the rhythm of the week before any nation existed.

The Seventh-day Adventist Church sets out this teaching in Fundamental Belief 20, which describes the Sabbath as a memorial of Creation. That is a beautiful way to think about it. In a world that often tells us we are accidents, every Saturday becomes a weekly reminder that we did not make ourselves. Someone made us on purpose, loves us deeply, and invites us to rest in His care.

## 2. God placed the Sabbath in the heart of the Ten Commandments

Centuries later, when God rescued Israel from slavery in Egypt, He gathered them at Mount Sinai and spoke the Ten Commandments aloud. Then He wrote them on tablets of stone with His own finger, something He did with no other part of the law. Right in the middle of those ten, the fourth commandment named a specific day.

> "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God." Exodus 20:8 to 10, KJV

Look closely at the very first word: remember. God was not introducing something new at Sinai. He was calling His people back to something He had already established, something their long years of slavery may have caused them to forget. The commandment even explains why in verse 11, pointing straight back to Creation, when the Lord made heaven and earth in six days and rested on the seventh.

Most Christians agree that the other nine commandments still guide us today. We still believe that lying, stealing, murder, adultery, and idolatry are wrong, and we teach our children to honor their parents. Adventists simply ask a gentle question: why would the one commandment that begins with the word "remember" be the one we are free to forget? Jesus connected love and obedience when He said, "If ye love me, keep my commandments" (John 14:15). Obedience is not how we earn His love. It is how we respond to it.

## 3. Jesus kept the Sabbath and called Himself its Lord

If anyone had the authority to set the Sabbath aside, it was Jesus. Yet the Gospels show Him keeping it faithfully, week after week, throughout His ministry. He never treated the Sabbath as something to throw away. He treated it as something to rescue from the burdens people had placed on it.

Luke tells us that when Jesus came to Nazareth, He went into the synagogue on the Sabbath day "as his custom was" (Luke 4:16). Sabbath worship was His regular habit, not an occasional visit. The Son of God, who had been present at Creation, spent His seventh days among God's people, reading Scripture and teaching.

At the same time, Jesus pushed back hard against the heavy human rules that religious leaders had piled onto the day. Some had turned the Sabbath into a list of restrictions so detailed that it felt more like a burden than a blessing. Jesus healed on the Sabbath, allowed His hungry disciples to pick grain, and taught that "it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days" (Matthew 12:12). He was not abolishing the Sabbath. He was restoring it to what God always intended: a day of healing, mercy, freedom, and joy.

He also called Himself "Lord also of the sabbath" (Mark 2:28). That title carries real weight. If Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath, then the Sabbath is, in a very real sense, the Lord's Day. Keeping it is a way of honoring Him as the Creator who made us and the Redeemer who restores us.

Even at the end of His earthly life, His followers honored the day. After the crucifixion, the women who loved Him prepared spices but "rested the sabbath day according to the commandment" (Luke 23:56). Then they came to the tomb early on the first day of the week (Luke 24:1). Scripture marks three days in a row here: the preparation day when Jesus died, the Sabbath when He rested in the tomb, and the first day when He rose. Even in death, Jesus rested on the seventh day, just as He had at Creation.

## 4. The apostles kept worshiping on the Sabbath after the resurrection

If the resurrection had moved worship from Saturday to Sunday, we would expect the book of Acts to tell us so. Acts records the life of the early church for roughly three decades after Jesus rose, and it is full of details about where and when the believers gathered. What we actually find is the apostles meeting on the Sabbath, year after year, in city after city.

When Paul and Barnabas arrived in Antioch of Pisidia, they went to the synagogue on the Sabbath and preached Christ. The Gentiles who heard them asked to hear more "the next sabbath," and on that following Sabbath nearly the whole city came together to hear the word of God (Acts 13:14, 42, 44). If Sunday had already become the Christian day of worship, this would have been the perfect moment to invite those Gentiles back the very next morning. Instead, they waited a full week for the Sabbath.

The pattern continues throughout Paul's travels. In Philippi, where there was no synagogue at all, Paul and his companions went out on the Sabbath to a riverside place where people gathered for prayer, and there Lydia believed (Acts 16:13). In Thessalonica, Paul reasoned with the people from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths, "as his manner was" (Acts 17:2), the same phrase Luke used about Jesus. In Corinth, he taught every Sabbath for a year and a half, persuading both Jews and Greeks (Acts 18:4, 11).

The New Testament also looks forward rather than backward. Hebrews 4:9 says, "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God." The Greek word used there is sabbatismos, which literally means a Sabbath keeping. And the prophet Isaiah pictures the redeemed in the new earth coming to worship God "from one sabbath to another" (Isaiah 66:22 to 23). The Sabbath began in Eden, and Scripture shows it continuing into eternity.

## 5. The Sabbath is a sign of freedom and belonging

When Moses repeated the Ten Commandments to a new generation in Deuteronomy, he gave a second reason to keep the Sabbath. Alongside Creation, he pointed to redemption: "remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 5:15). Slaves in Egypt never got a day off. Free people do. The Sabbath was a weekly celebration that God had broken their chains.

For Christians, that deliverance points straight to Jesus, who frees us from the slavery of sin and fear. God calls the Sabbath a sign "that ye may know that I am the LORD your God" (Ezekiel 20:20). Think of it like a wedding ring. Wearing a ring does not make you married, and taking it off does not end the marriage. But the ring is a visible, daily sign of a relationship and a promise. The Sabbath works the same way between God and His people.

This is exactly why Adventists insist that Sabbath keeping is never about earning salvation. We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus alone, and not by our own works (Ephesians 2:8 to 9). In fact, resting on the Sabbath is one of the clearest pictures of grace there is. Once a week we stop working, stop striving, and stop trying to prove ourselves. We trust God to hold our lives together while we rest, which is what faith looks like in practice.

## So how did most Christians end up worshiping on Sunday?

If the Bible is this consistent about the seventh day, it is natural to ask how most of the Christian world came to worship on Sunday. The honest answer is that the shift came gradually over several centuries, through church tradition and civil law, rather than through a command in Scripture. Many historians, including Catholic and Protestant scholars, describe Sunday observance as a development of the centuries after the apostles.

In the second century, some Christians began gathering on Sunday to honor the resurrection. Many historians link the growing preference for Sunday to a desire to separate the church from Judaism during a time when Jews faced suspicion and hostility from the Roman empire. Over time, what began as an additional gathering in some places slowly replaced the Sabbath in others.

Civil law then reinforced the change. On March 7, 321, Emperor Constantine issued the first known civil law calling for rest on "the venerable day of the sun," with an exception allowing farmers to keep working. Later in the fourth century, the regional Council of Laodicea instructed Christians to work on Saturday and to honor Sunday instead. Notice that the council needed to say this at all, which shows that many believers were still keeping the seventh day.

- Creation: God rests on the seventh day: He blesses the day and sets it apart as holy for all humanity (Genesis 2:2 to 3).

- Mount Sinai: The fourth commandment: God writes "Remember the sabbath day" with His own finger (Exodus 20:8 to 11).

- Jesus' ministry: The Lord of the Sabbath: Jesus worships on the Sabbath "as his custom was" and restores its true meaning (Luke 4:16).

- The early church: Apostles keep the Sabbath: Paul preaches on the Sabbath to Jews and Gentiles across the Roman world (Acts 13 to 18).

- Second century: Sunday gatherings grow: Some Christians begin meeting on Sunday as tension with Judaism and Rome rises.

- AD 321: Constantine's Sunday law: The first civil law calls for rest on "the venerable day of the sun."

- Fourth century: Council of Laodicea: Christians are told to work on Saturday and honor Sunday instead.

- 1840s: The Sabbath restored: Early Adventists learn the seventh day Sabbath from Seventh Day Baptists and embrace it.

Throughout those centuries and beyond, faithful groups of believers in many lands continued to keep the Sabbath, and the practice never fully disappeared. In the 1840s, the founders of the Adventist movement learned the seventh day Sabbath from Seventh Day Baptists, studied the Scriptures carefully, and became convinced it was a truth worth restoring for the church in the last days.

It is important to say this clearly: Adventists do not believe that Christians who worship on Sunday are insincere or less loved by God. Millions of faithful believers worship on Sunday with all their hearts, and God sees every one of them. The question Adventists raise is not about anyone's sincerity. It is simply this: what does Scripture itself say, and will we follow it wherever it leads?

## Is Saturday really the seventh day?

Yes, and this is easier to confirm than many people expect. The weekly cycle has never been broken. When the Gregorian calendar replaced the older Julian calendar in 1582, ten dates were dropped to correct the calendar's drift, but the days of the week stayed in perfect order. Thursday, October 4 was followed by Friday, October 15. The dates changed, but the week did not.

The Jewish people have also kept the seventh day continuously since ancient times, which provides a living witness to which day the Sabbath falls on. Jesus kept the same weekly Sabbath as the Jewish community of His day, and that same day continues to come around every Saturday.

Language tells the story too. In many languages around the world, the name for Saturday comes directly from the word Sabbath. Spanish says sábado, Italian says sabato, and French says samedi. In Haitian Creole, Saturday is samdi, a word that traces back through French and Latin to the Sabbath. Many Haitian families have been naming the Sabbath every single week without realizing it.

## Honest questions people ask

Whenever this topic comes up, a few Bible passages are usually raised as evidence that the Sabbath has changed. These are fair questions, and they deserve careful answers rather than quick dismissals. Here is how Adventists understand each one.

| Passage | What it describes | What it does not say |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acts 20:7 | A farewell meeting, likely Saturday night, before Paul left | That the first day became holy |
| 1 Corinthians 16:2 | Setting aside relief money at home | That a worship service was held |
| Colossians 2:16 | Yearly ceremonial feasts that pointed to Christ | That the Creation Sabbath ended |
| Romans 14:5 | Disputes over food and fast days | Anything about the Sabbath |
| Revelation 1:10 | John in the Spirit on the Lord's day | That the Lord's day is Sunday |

### Does Acts 20:7 show the early church met on Sunday?

Acts 20:7 describes a farewell meeting in the city of Troas on the first day of the week, when Paul preached until midnight because he was leaving the next morning. In biblical reckoning, the first day of the week began at sunset on Saturday, so this was most likely a Saturday night gathering, and Paul set out on his journey on Sunday morning. The passage also mentions breaking bread, which the believers did daily according to Acts 2:46. Acts 20:7 faithfully records a special event, but it never commands a new day of worship or calls the first day holy.

### What about 1 Corinthians 16:2?

In this verse Paul asked believers to set money aside "by him in store" on the first day of the week, as an offering for famine relief for the struggling believers in Jerusalem. The wording points to each person setting funds aside at home before the week's spending began, so that the gift would be ready when Paul arrived and no collection would be needed then. It is a practical plan for gathering relief offerings, and it does not describe a worship service or mention any change to the Sabbath.

### Doesn't Colossians 2:16 say the Sabbath no longer matters?

Colossians 2:16 to 17 mentions "holy days," "new moon," and "sabbath days," and calls them a shadow of things to come. Adventists understand this list as the yearly ceremonial feasts of Israel and their special sabbaths, which were tied to the sacrificial system and pointed forward to Christ's sacrifice. The same grouping of feasts, new moons, and sabbaths appears in Old Testament passages about temple offerings, such as Ezekiel 45:17. The weekly Sabbath is different, because it points back to Creation rather than forward to the cross, and something that began in a sinless Eden could not be a shadow of a remedy for sin.

### Doesn't Romans 14:5 say every day is alike?

Romans 14 deals with disputes among believers over food and over certain days connected with fasting and feasting. The word Sabbath does not appear anywhere in the chapter. Paul's point is that Christians should stop judging one another over personal customs and matters of conscience. Reading the chapter as a quiet cancellation of one of the Ten Commandments would ask far more of it than Paul ever intended.

### Isn't Sunday the Lord's Day because of the resurrection?

The resurrection is the heart of the gospel, and Adventists celebrate it with great joy. Without it, our faith would be empty. Yet the New Testament gives baptism, not a new weekly day, as the memorial of the death, burial, and resurrection of Jesus (Romans 6:4). When John writes that he was in the Spirit on "the Lord's day" (Revelation 1:10), the rest of Scripture helps us identify which day the Lord calls His own. God calls the Sabbath "my holy day" (Isaiah 58:13), and Jesus calls Himself Lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28).

## What Sabbath actually looks like

Many people imagine the Sabbath as a long list of things you are not allowed to do. In practice, for most Adventist families, it feels much more like a weekly holiday with God and the people you love. It is the day the whole week leans toward.

- Friday : Prepare the home and meals
- Sunset : Family worship begins the Sabbath
- Morning : Sabbath School and worship
- Afternoon : Nature, service, fellowship
- Saturday sunset : Close with prayer

Isaiah invites us to "call the sabbath a delight" (Isaiah 58:13), and that word captures the spirit of it well. For many families, Friday becomes a day of preparation, with the house tidied, the meals cooked ahead, and the errands finished. As the sun sets, the family gathers for a simple worship with songs, a Bible reading, and prayer. Phones and screens are set aside, and a warm meal is shared without the usual rush.

Saturday morning brings Sabbath School, where people of every age study the Bible together in small classes, followed by the main worship service with music, prayer, and preaching. The afternoon is open time with God. Families might take a walk in nature, visit someone who is sick or lonely, read together, or simply enjoy long conversations around the table. Work, shopping, and the usual chase of the week pause until sunset, and the quiet itself becomes a gift.

At Shekinah in Alvarado, Sabbath School begins at 10:00 AM and the Divine Service at 11:00 AM, with worship in Kreyòl and English. After the service, the church family shares a meal together, and visitors are always welcome at the table. For many Haitian families, the Sabbath table is where faith, culture, and community meet, and where the joy of the day is easiest to feel.

Related: [What Happens When You Die? What the Bible Really Teaches](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/what-happens-when-you-die-bible/)

## Reflection questions

Take a few quiet minutes with these questions, either on your own or with someone you trust. First, ask yourself what would change in your week if you set aside 24 hours to rest in God without any guilt. Then consider whether your view of the Sabbath has come from what Scripture actually says, or mostly from what you have always heard. Finally, think about how a weekly day of rest might remind you that your worth comes from God's love rather than from how much you get done.

## A word of encouragement

If this is all new to you, there is no need to settle every question today. God is patient with honest seekers, and He meets each of us where we are. The Sabbath is not a burden He places on tired shoulders. It is an invitation from a Savior who said, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28).

Open your Bible, read these passages for yourself, and ask Him to guide you. Talk with Him about what you find. The same God who rested on the seventh day at Creation still longs to spend time with you, and He has set aside a whole day every week for exactly that.

## A prayer

Lord, thank You for making us and for loving us before we did anything to deserve it. Thank You for giving us a day to stop, to breathe, and to remember that we belong to You. When our weeks feel crowded and our hearts feel tired, teach us to rest in You. Help me read Your Word with an open heart, and lead me into the rest that only Jesus can give. Amen.

## Your next step

We would love to welcome you for your very first Sabbath. Come as you are on Saturday morning to 205 E Carver St in Alvarado, Texas. A friendly greeter will meet you at the door and help you find a seat, and you are warmly invited to stay for lunch with our church family afterward. If you would rather study first, you can request a free Bible study below and explore these passages one on one, at your own pace, with someone who would be glad to walk with you.

- Source: [What Is the Sabbath, Adventist.org](https://www.adventist.org/the-sabbath/)

- Source: [What We Believe: The 28 Fundamental Beliefs, Adventist.org](https://www.adventist.org/beliefs/)

- Source: [Why Do Adventists Worship on Saturday, Ask an Adventist Friend](https://www.askanadventistfriend.com/adventist-beliefs/sabbath/why-do-adventists-worship-on-saturday/)

- Source: [The Holy Bible, King James Version](https://www.kingjamesbibleonline.org/)

> "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." Exodus 20:8, KJV

# Resting in His Presence: What the Sabbath Teaches Us About Trust

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/resting-in-his-presence-what-the-sabbath-teaches-us-about-trust/
Category: Devotional
Author: Ellen Dove
Published: 2026-10-19

Sabbath rest is a weekly act of trust that reminds us our worth comes from God, not our productivity, and it begins with preparing our homes and hearts before Friday sunset.


It is Friday afternoon and the list is still long. There are emails you meant to answer, groceries you have not bought, a sink full of dishes, and a quiet voice in the back of your mind saying that if you stop now, everything will fall apart. Many of us know that feeling well. We have learned to measure a good week by how much we finished, and a good life by how busy we stayed.

Into that pressure, God speaks a surprising word. Once every seven days He invites us to put the work down before it is all done, to let the unanswered messages wait, and to rest anyway. That invitation can feel almost uncomfortable at first, because it asks us to believe something our culture rarely tells us. It asks us to believe that God can hold our lives together for a whole day while we let go of the controls.

This article is not mainly about which day the Sabbath falls on, since we have written about that separately. Here we want to sit with a quieter question that many tired believers ask. What does the Sabbath teach us about trusting God, and how can we prepare our homes and hearts to receive that rest each week?

## The short answer

- 6 days : Israel gathered manna, with a double portion on the sixth
- 0 : Manna found in the field on the seventh day
- 24 hours : Of holy time, from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset

The Sabbath is a weekly act of trust. When we stop working on the seventh day, we are saying with our whole lives that God is our provider, that our worth does not come from our productivity, and that the world is safe in His hands even when we are not running it. Scripture shows this most clearly in the story of the manna, in the words of Jesus to the weary, and in the invitation of Hebrews 4 to enter God's rest by faith.

The Seventh-day Adventist Church describes the Sabbath in Fundamental Belief 20 as a memorial of Creation and a day of rest, worship, and ministry, and calls it "a day of delightful communion with God and one another." That phrase is worth holding onto. Rest is not simply the absence of work. It is the presence of God, received with open hands.

Related: [Why Do Seventh-day Adventists Worship on Saturday?](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/why-do-seventh-day-adventists-worship-on-saturday/)

## Learning trust in the wilderness: the manna and the double portion

One of the first places the Bible names the Sabbath is not on a mountain but in a desert, around the breakfast table. In Exodus 16, a hungry nation fresh out of slavery feared they would starve. God answered with bread from heaven and attached a lesson that would shape them for forty years.

> "Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you; and the people shall go out and gather a certain rate every day, that I may prove them, whether they will walk in my law, or no." Exodus 16:4, KJV

Notice the word "prove." God was teaching them to trust Him one day at a time. When some tried to save extra overnight, it "bred worms, and stank" (Exodus 16:20). Hoarding did not work, because the point was never self sufficiency but dependence on a faithful Provider.

Then came the sixth day. God told them that on that day they would gather "twice as much" (Exodus 16:5), and Moses explained why: "To morrow is the rest of the holy sabbath unto the LORD" (Exodus 16:23). The manna that spoiled on every other night stayed fresh through the Sabbath. Some people still went out on the seventh day to look for more, "and they found none" (Exodus 16:27). God's provision on Friday was enough for Saturday too.

> "See, for that the LORD hath given you the sabbath, therefore he giveth you on the sixth day the bread of two days." Exodus 16:29, KJV

This is the heart of Sabbath trust. God provides first, and then He invites us to stop. Every Friday, when we lay down what is unfinished, we stand where Israel stood, holding the double portion and believing that God has already given enough.

## Your worth is not measured by your work

Many of us carry a quiet belief that we are only as valuable as what we produce, so rest feels like something we must earn. The Sabbath gently breaks that lie. Think about the order of Creation. Humanity was made on the sixth day, and the very first full day Adam and Eve experienced was the seventh day, when "God ended his work which he had made; and he rested" (Genesis 2:2). Before they had tended the garden through a single season or gathered a single harvest, God gave them rest. They did not begin their lives working toward rest. They began their lives resting in what God had already finished.

Jesus made the same point when religious leaders turned the Sabbath into a heavy list of rules: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath" (Mark 2:27). The Sabbath is a gift shaped around human need. Once a week God reminds you that you are His child before you are His worker, loved even on the days you accomplish nothing.

**What Sabbath rest says about God**
- He provides before He asks us to stop (Exodus 16:29)
- He made rest for our good (Mark 2:27)
- He finished His work, so we can cease from ours (Hebrews 4:10)
- He welcomes the weary, not only the strong (Matthew 11:28)

## Come unto Me: rest for the weary

Some of the most tender words Jesus ever spoke were not addressed to the impressive or the successful. They were an invitation to anyone carrying more than they could bear. If that describes you this week, these words are for you.

> "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls." Matthew 11:28 to 29, KJV

Jesus does not offer rest as a technique. He offers Himself. The rest He gives reaches deeper than the body, into the soul, where worry and guilt and striving live. It is meaningful that Matthew places these words right before two Sabbath stories in chapter 12, where Jesus defends His hungry disciples and heals a man on the Sabbath, declaring that "it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days" (Matthew 12:12). Many Bible readers see that placement as intentional, showing that the Sabbath is one of the ways Jesus gives His rest to us.

So when the Sabbath begins, it is not just the calendar that changes. It is an appointment with the Savior who said "Come," and we come not to prove our faithfulness but because our souls need what only He can give. That is a very different way to enter a weekend.

## Entering His rest by faith: Hebrews 4

Hebrews looks back at the Israelites in the wilderness and asks why so many never entered the rest God promised. Its answer is simple and searching: unbelief. They saw a miracle every morning in the manna, yet never fully trusted the One who sent it.

> "There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his." Hebrews 4:9 to 10, KJV

Here the writer connects the rest of salvation with the rest of the seventh day. To enter God's rest is to stop trying to save ourselves and to trust the finished work of Christ. Hebrews 4:3 says it plainly: "we which have believed do enter into rest." The weekly Sabbath becomes a living picture of that deeper rest, a sample every seven days of what it means to cease from our own works and lean fully on grace.

We should be careful to separate text from interpretation here. The Bible directly says that a rest remains for God's people and that it is entered by faith, while Adventist teachers understand the weekly Sabbath as a sign and foretaste of that rest of grace. Keeping the Sabbath does not earn salvation; it is one of the clearest ways we practice the trust that salvation invites.

## Preparing your home and heart before sunset

If the manna story teaches anything practical, it is that Sabbath rest begins with preparation. Israel had to gather the double portion on the sixth day and "bake that which ye will bake to day" (Exodus 16:23). The Gospels also call Friday "the preparation," and Luke notes that on the day Jesus died "the sabbath drew on" (Luke 23:54). Rest that is planned is usually rest that is received.

- Earlier in the week : Plan meals and errands so Friday is not a rush
- Friday morning : Cook ahead and tidy the spaces you will share
- Friday afternoon : Finish or set aside work, then silence the noise
- Sunset : Gather for songs, Scripture, and prayer
- Saturday : Worship, rest, nature, and time with people you love

It helps to spread the work across the week. A family resource from the Seventh-day Adventist Ministerial Association suggests planning Sabbath meals early, doing laundry midweek, and shopping and cooking ahead on Thursday so Friday holds only the final touches. The goal is to arrive at sunset ready to stop, not scrambling to finish.

Preparing the heart matters just as much. Before sunset, make things right with anyone you have hurt during the week, and hand your worries to God, casting "all your care upon him; for he careth for you" (1 Peter 5:7). Some families light a candle, sing a hymn, or step outside to watch the sky change color as holy time begins.

### What if my week does not allow perfect preparation?

Some weeks a child gets sick or a shift runs late. The Sabbath is not ruined by an imperfect Friday, because the rest is God's gift, not our achievement. Do what you reasonably can, let the rest go, and enter the day with gratitude rather than guilt.

## What trusting rest can look like on the Sabbath

Once the Sabbath begins, the hardest part is often the letting go. The urge to check the phone or plan Monday can be strong. Each time we set it aside, we practice the trust Israel practiced when they left their baskets empty on the seventh morning.

| Instead of | Try this on the Sabbath |
| --- | --- |
| Checking work messages | Leaving the phone in another room for worship and meals |
| Catching up on chores | Enjoying the home you prepared the day before |
| Worrying about next week | Reading a psalm and praying over the worry |
| Rushing through meals | Lingering at the table with family and guests |
| Staying indoors alone | Walking in nature or visiting someone who is lonely |

The Sabbath is also meant to be shared. Isaiah invites us to "call the sabbath a delight" (Isaiah 58:13), and delight often comes in community. At Shekinah in Alvarado, worship is in Kreyòl and English, and the church family shares a meal after the service, where Sabbath rest becomes something you can taste and feel.

## Questions people ask

### What does the Sabbath teach us about trusting God?

The Sabbath teaches us to trust God as our provider, because stopping our work on the seventh day says that our worth does not come from our productivity and that the world is safe in His hands even when we are not running it. Israel learned this in Exodus 16, where God gave a double portion of manna on the sixth day and none was found in the field on the seventh. Jesus offered the same rest to the weary in Matthew 11:28 to 29, and Hebrews 4 invites us to enter God's rest by faith. Every Friday, when we lay down unfinished work, we stand where Israel stood, believing God has already given enough.

### When does the Sabbath start and end?

The Sabbath begins at sunset on Friday and ends at sunset on Saturday, a full 24 hours of holy time. Seventh-day Adventists keep this seventh day as a memorial of Creation and a day of rest, worship, and ministry, as described in Fundamental Belief 20. The Gospels call Friday "the preparation," and Luke 23:54 notes that on the day Jesus died "the sabbath drew on." Many families mark the moment with songs, Scripture, and prayer as the sun goes down.

### How do you prepare for the Sabbath?

You prepare for the Sabbath by spreading the work across the week and then preparing your heart before sunset on Friday. A family resource from the Seventh-day Adventist Ministerial Association suggests planning Sabbath meals early, doing laundry midweek, and shopping and cooking ahead on Thursday so Friday holds only the final touches. Before sunset, make things right with anyone you have hurt during the week, and hand your worries to God as 1 Peter 5:7 invites. Rest that is planned is usually rest that is received.

### Does keeping the Sabbath earn salvation?

No, keeping the Sabbath does not earn salvation; it is one of the clearest ways we practice the trust that salvation invites. Hebrews 4:3 says that "we which have believed do enter into rest," and Hebrews 4:10 describes that rest as ceasing from our own works as God did from His. The Bible directly says that a rest remains for God's people and that it is entered by faith, while Adventist teachers understand the weekly Sabbath as a sign and foretaste of that rest of grace. Jesus also said that "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath" (Mark 2:27), which shows that the day is a gift rather than a burden.

## Reflection questions

Take a quiet moment with these questions this week. What is one thing you find hardest to leave unfinished when the Sabbath begins, and what might that reveal about where you place your trust? How might your view of yourself change if you truly believed your worth comes from God's love rather than from what you accomplish? And what is one small step you could take this Friday to prepare your home and heart before sunset?

## A word of encouragement

If rest feels difficult for you, you are not failing. The Israelites needed forty years of manna to learn trust, and God was patient with them every morning. He is patient with you too, and the Sabbath is a gift you can open again every seven days.

Remember that the One who invites you to rest is the same One who provides the double portion. He has already given enough. When the sun sets this Friday, you can put the work down, take a deep breath, and say with the psalmist, "I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety" (Psalm 4:8).

## A prayer

Faithful Father, thank You for providing for me before I even ask. Forgive me for the times I have trusted my own effort more than Your care. Teach me to prepare my home and my heart for Your holy day, and when the sun goes down, help me to truly let go. Let me find in Jesus the rest my soul has been looking for, and let my Sabbath be a delight to You. Amen.

## Your next step

If you would like to explore the rest Jesus offers more deeply, we would be glad to study with you. Request a free Bible study and go through these passages one on one, at your own pace. And if you are near Alvarado, you are warmly welcome at 205 E Carver St, where Sabbath School begins at 10:00 AM and the Divine Service at 11:00 AM.

# Five Ways to Build Faith at the Dinner Table

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/five-ways-to-build-faith-at-the-dinner-table/
Category: Devotional
Author: Grace Mitchell
Published: 2026-10-12

Faith grows at home through small moments repeated often, and five simple habits can turn your dinner table into a place where children meet God.


The plates are on the table, someone is already reaching for the rice, a phone buzzes, and a child is telling a story about school that has no clear ending. It is not exactly a quiet, holy scene. Yet for many families, this messy moment is the one time each day when everyone is in the same room. That makes the dinner table one of the most important places in the home.

Many parents feel a quiet guilt about family worship. They imagine a long, structured devotional with songs, a lesson, and children sitting perfectly still, and when that feels out of reach, it is easy to do nothing. The Bible paints a much simpler and more hopeful picture of how faith passes from one generation to the next.

This article offers five small, repeatable ways to build faith at the dinner table. None takes more than a few minutes or requires perfect children. What they require is something every family can give: consistency, honesty, and a willingness to let God into the rhythm of a meal.

## The short answer

- 5 : Simple habits for any family table
- 5 minutes : Is often enough to begin
- 1 verse : Can shape a whole conversation

Faith grows at home most naturally through small moments repeated often, not through rare, impressive events. Scripture calls parents to talk about God's words "when thou sittest in thine house" (Deuteronomy 6:7), and few places capture sitting in the house better than the family table. Five simple practices can turn that table into a place of worship: sharing a blessing, praying for a neighbor by name, reading one verse and asking the youngest, telling stories of God's faithfulness, and making room for guests.

The Seventh-day Adventist Church teaches in Fundamental Belief 23 that parents are to bring up their children to love and obey the Lord. The Adventist Department of Family Ministries describes family worship not as something to force on anyone, but as an opportunity to strengthen relationships with one another and with God. That is exactly the spirit of these five ideas.

## Why the table matters so much

When God gave Israel His words through Moses, He did not tell parents to save faith for the temple or for special occasions. He placed it right in the middle of daily life. The words are simple enough for any parent to understand.

> "And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." Deuteronomy 6:6 to 7, KJV

Notice the order. The words must first be "in thine heart" before they can be taught, because children learn more from what we love than from what we say. Then notice the setting: sitting, walking, lying down, rising up. God built the passing on of faith into the most ordinary moments of family life, and mealtime is one of the clearest.

Jesus often revealed God's love around a table. After His resurrection, two discouraged disciples recognized Him only when He sat at meat with them and "took bread, and blessed it, and brake, and gave to them. And their eyes were opened, and they knew him" (Luke 24:30 to 31). The early church also met "breaking bread from house to house" (Acts 2:46). The table has always been a place where people meet Jesus.

**What makes table faith work**
- Short and simple beats long and rare
- Consistency matters more than perfection
- Let children participate, not just listen
- Keep it warm, never forced or used as punishment

## Five ways to build faith at the dinner table

### 1. Share a blessing before you eat

The simplest place to begin is with thanks. Before the first bite, pause together and thank God for the food and for one another. Jesus modeled this when He "had given thanks" before distributing the loaves (John 6:11), and Paul encourages us, "In every thing give thanks" (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

To make the blessing more than a routine, invite each person to name one specific thing they are thankful for that day. A child might name sunshine at recess, and a parent might be grateful simply that everyone is home. Over time, this trains the whole family to notice God's goodness, echoing the psalmist: "Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits" (Psalm 103:2).

In many Haitian homes, blessing the food is already a cherished habit, sometimes prayed in Kreyòl by a grandparent. If that is part of your family story, keep it alive. Let the children hear the prayers of the older generation, and let them pray in the language of their heart too.

### 2. Pray for a neighbor by name

Faith grows when it looks outward. A powerful habit is to pray together for one specific person outside the home, by name. It might be a neighbor down the street, a classmate who seems lonely, a coworker going through a hard time, or a relative back in Haiti.

Scripture calls us to pray for others. Paul urged that "supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men" (1 Timothy 2:1). When God's people were living as exiles far from home, He told them to "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it" (Jeremiah 29:7). That verse can speak especially to immigrant families who are learning to love a new community while still carrying their homeland in their hearts.

Praying by name helps children understand that prayer is a real conversation with a God who cares about real people. It also opens the door to action. A family that prays for a lonely neighbor on Monday might bake bread for that neighbor on Thursday.

- Choose : Pick one person outside your home to pray for this week
- Name : Say their name aloud in prayer at dinner
- Notice : Ask each other what that person might need
- Act : Find one small way to show them kindness
- Follow up : Share what happened at a later meal

### 3. Read one verse and ask the youngest

Family Bible reading does not need to be long to be meaningful. Choose one short verse, read it aloud, and then ask the youngest person at the table a simple question about it. What do you think this means? Who in this verse needs help? What does this tell us about God?

Starting with the youngest keeps the conversation simple, shows little ones their thoughts matter, and invites older family members to listen instead of lecture. Jesus said, "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God" (Mark 10:14). Sometimes a four year old's simple answer opens a deeper conversation than any adult could plan.

Scripture also expects children to ask questions about faith. Moses wrote, "And when thy son asketh thee in time to come, saying, What mean the testimonies, and the statutes, and the judgments" (Deuteronomy 6:20), and then told parents to answer with the story of how God saved them. Questions are not a threat to faith. They are an invitation to share it.

| Verse to read | A question for the youngest |
| --- | --- |
| Psalm 119:105 | What does a lamp help us do in the dark? |
| John 6:35 | Why do you think Jesus called Himself bread? |
| Psalm 23:2 | Where is your favorite peaceful place? |
| Proverbs 15:17 | What makes a meal feel full of love? |
| 1 Peter 5:7 | What is one worry you can give to God tonight? |

### 4. Tell stories of God's faithfulness

Every family has stories of times when God provided, protected, or answered prayer. These stories are some of the most precious things a family can pass down. Scripture says, "We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done" (Psalm 78:4).

Once a week or so, invite someone to share a story: how grandparents came to know Jesus, how the family found its way to a new country, or a time when money was short and God made a way. Keep the stories honest and short. Children who hear them begin to see their own lives as part of a bigger story God is writing.

Many Haitian families carry rich stories of faith through hardship, migration, and new beginnings. Telling those stories honestly, including the hard parts, helps children understand that faith is not pretending life is easy. It is trusting God in the middle of real life. Even the prophet Joel, describing a devastating locust plague, told the people, "Tell ye your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation" (Joel 1:3), because the hard chapters belong in the story too.

### 5. Make room for others at your table

The final way to build faith at the table is to open it. Inviting a guest, whether a neighbor, a new friend from church, a lonely student, or a family new to the area, teaches children that God's love is meant to be shared. Paul encouraged believers to be "given to hospitality" (Romans 12:13), and the early church grew around open homes and shared meals.

Hospitality does not require a fancy meal, and a simple pot of rice and beans served with warmth can be a meaningful gift. Proverbs reminds us, "Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith" (Proverbs 15:17). What guests remember is not the menu but the welcome.

At Shekinah in Alvarado, the church family shares a meal together after the Sabbath service, and visitors are welcome at the table. The Sabbath table at church and the dinner table at home can strengthen one another. Children who see the same welcome and faith in both places learn that hospitality is part of following Jesus.

## Proverbs 22:6 and the long view

Many parents hold onto a familiar promise: "Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it" (Proverbs 22:6). Proverbs are general principles of how life usually works under God's blessing, not guarantees that override a child's free choice. Even faithful parents sometimes watch a child wander.

What this verse does promise is that training matters. The small, repeated habits of childhood leave deep marks that often remain long after a child has grown up. A prayer heard a thousand times at the dinner table, a verse discussed over rice and beans, or a story of God's faithfulness told on a hard night can become a lifeline years later. Our role is to plant faithfully and to trust God with the harvest.

Related: [Diri ak Pwa the Healthy Way](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/diri-ak-pwa-the-healthy-way/)

## Getting started this week

You do not need to begin with all five habits at once, which can make family worship feel heavy. Choose one practice, perhaps the shared blessing, and do it every evening this week. When it feels natural, add a second.

Keep the tone warm and light. If a child is restless, keep it short, and if you miss a night, simply begin again. The goal is not a perfect program but a home where God is a natural part of the conversation and faith belongs at the table as surely as food does.

## Questions people ask

### How long should family devotions at the dinner table be?

Family devotions at the dinner table can be very short, and five minutes is often enough to begin. Short and simple habits repeated often matter more than long, rare, impressive events. If a child is restless, keep it short, and if you miss a night, simply begin again. The goal is not a perfect program but a home where God is a natural part of the conversation.

### How do you start family worship with young children?

The easiest way to start family worship with young children is to choose one simple habit, such as a shared blessing before dinner, and practice it every evening for a week before adding another. Let children participate rather than just listen, for example by naming one thing they are thankful for or answering a simple question about a short verse. Starting with the youngest person at the table shows little ones their thoughts matter, and Jesus welcomed children in Mark 10:14. Keep the tone warm and light, and never use family worship as punishment.

### What Bible verse talks about teaching children at home?

Deuteronomy 6:6 to 7 is the key Bible passage about teaching children at home, telling parents to talk of God's words "when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." The passage begins by saying these words must first be "in thine heart," because children learn more from what we love than from what we say. Psalm 78:4 adds the call of "shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD." Proverbs 22:6 also encourages parents to train up a child in the way he should go.

### Does Proverbs 22:6 guarantee my child will stay faithful?

No, Proverbs 22:6 is a general principle of how life usually works under God's blessing, not a guarantee that overrides a child's free choice. Even faithful parents sometimes watch a child wander. What the verse does promise is that training matters, because the small habits of childhood often leave deep marks long after a child has grown up. Our role is to plant faithfully and to trust God with the harvest.

## Reflection questions

Take a moment to think about your own family table. What does a typical meal in your home feel like right now, and where might there be space for even one minute of faith? Which of these five habits feels most natural for your family to begin this week? And what story of God's faithfulness from your own life would you most want your children or grandchildren to remember?

## A word of encouragement

If you feel like you have fallen short as a parent or grandparent, please hear this. God does not ask for perfect families. He asks for willing hearts. The same Jesus who welcomed restless children and broke bread with discouraged disciples is glad to sit at your table too, noise and spilled cups included.

Every small moment of faith you share is a seed, and some take years to sprout. None of them are wasted in God's hands. Keep showing up, keep praying, and trust Him to do what only He can do in the hearts of the people you love.

## A prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for the gift of family and for the food on our table. Come and sit with us at every meal. Help us to give thanks, to pray for our neighbors, to listen to our children, and to tell the stories of Your goodness. Where we feel tired or unsure, give us patience and joy. Let our home be a place where everyone who sits at our table can taste and see that You are good. Amen.

If you would like help building faith in your home, a free Bible study is a wonderful place to start, for yourself or together as a family. Request one below and study at your own pace with someone who cares. And if you are near Alvarado, we would love to welcome your family on Sabbath morning at 205 E Carver St and invite you to stay for our shared meal.
