# Walk With Me: Starting a Sabbath Afternoon Walking Group

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/walk-with-me-starting-a-sabbath-afternoon-walking-group/
Category: Health
Author: David Carter
Published: 2026-09-07

Walking is one of the simplest ways to care for the body God gave you, and a gentle Sabbath afternoon walk with others can turn exercise into fellowship and worship.


The Sabbath meal is finished, the plates are stacked, and the afternoon stretches out ahead like an open field. Some of the family are drifting toward the couch, the children are getting restless, and someone suggests a nap. Then another voice says, "Why don't we go for a walk?" It is such a simple idea, and yet that one question can turn a sleepy afternoon into one of the sweetest hours of the week.

Walking is the kind of exercise almost anyone can start. It needs no gym membership, no special skill, and very little equipment beyond a comfortable pair of shoes. When you walk with others, it becomes something more than exercise. It becomes conversation, friendship, and, on the Sabbath, a quiet way to enjoy the world God made.

This guide covers what health experts say about the benefits of walking and how much activity adults need. It also looks at what the Bible says about walking and nature on the Sabbath, and how a family, a group of friends, or a small church group can start a Sabbath afternoon walk. It is general health education, so if you have a medical condition or have not been active for a while, please check with your doctor before you begin.

## The short answer

- 150 minutes : Weekly moderate activity the CDC recommends for adults
- 30 minutes : One way to get there: 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week
- 60 minutes : Daily activity youth ages 6 to 17 need (HHS)

The CDC recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity each week, and it names brisk walking as an example of moderate activity. You do not have to do it all at once. The CDC suggests that 30 minutes a day on five days a week is one simple way to reach the goal, and some physical activity is better than none.

Spiritually, a Sabbath afternoon walk fits beautifully with the purpose of the day. Jesus walked through fields with His disciples on the Sabbath, and Scripture invites us to see God's glory in creation. A gentle walk together, with conversation and gratitude, can be a restful way to honor the Lord of the Sabbath rather than a break from Him.

## The benefits of walking

Health organizations agree that walking is one of the most accessible forms of exercise there is. Mayo Clinic lists a wide range of benefits that come from regular walking. It can help you maintain a healthy weight, prevent or manage conditions such as heart disease, stroke, high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, and some cancers, improve heart health and endurance, and strengthen bones and muscles.

Mayo Clinic also notes that walking can boost energy, improve mood, thinking, memory, and sleep, and reduce stress and anxiety. For older adults, it can improve physical function and lower the risk of falls. The American Heart Association likewise says walking can have a significant impact on your health by lowering your chances of heart disease. The Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans add that some benefits come right away, since physical activity has immediate benefits such as reducing anxiety and blood pressure and improving the quality of sleep.

**What regular walking can do**
- Support a healthy weight
- Lower the risk of heart disease, stroke, and type 2 diabetes
- Strengthen bones and muscles
- Lift mood and reduce stress
- Improve sleep and energy
- Help older adults lower fall risk

The guidelines also make a point that encourages beginners. The first key guideline for adults is simply to move more and sit less, and any amount of physical activity has some health benefits. If you have not exercised in years, you do not need to start at 150 minutes. A short walk after lunch counts, and so does every step you add from there.

## How much walking do you need?

The federal Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans recommend that adults get at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate intensity aerobic activity each week. The CDC adds that adults also benefit from muscle strengthening activity on at least two days a week. For children and teens, the guidelines call for at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity every day for ages 6 through 17.

| Who | Weekly goal | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adults | At least 150 minutes of moderate activity, such as brisk walking | CDC |
| Adults | Muscle strengthening at least 2 days a week | CDC |
| Youth ages 6 to 17 | At least 60 minutes of activity every day | HHS guidelines |
| Everyone | Move more and sit less; any amount helps | HHS guidelines |

How brisk is brisk? Harvard Health offers a simple talk test. Walk as if you are in a bit of a hurry, so that your breathing speeds up but you can still talk in full sentences. That pace is perfect for a group walk, because it keeps everyone moving while still leaving room for conversation.

## What the Bible says about walking

Walking is one of the Bible's favorite pictures of a life lived with God. Enoch is remembered in a single, unforgettable line: "And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him" (Genesis 5:24). To walk with someone is to share the same pace, direction, and company, which is a picture of friendship.

### God walked in the garden

The first walk in Scripture belongs to God Himself. After Adam and Eve sinned, they heard Him coming toward them in the evening. The moment is both sad and revealing.

> "And they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the Lord God amongst the trees of the garden." Genesis 3:8, KJV

The first couple hid, yet the verse reveals something lovely about God's heart. The text suggests that walking in the garden in the cool of the day was a natural setting for God to meet with the people He made. Many readers have seen in this a glimpse of the fellowship God intended from the beginning, unhurried time together in the beauty of creation.

### Strength for the journey

Isaiah offers one of the most loved promises in all of Scripture. It was first spoken to God's people in a weary season. It still speaks to anyone who feels tired and worn down.

> "But they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint." Isaiah 40:31, KJV

The prophet is speaking about spiritual strength that comes from trusting God, not giving fitness advice. Still, the picture fits a walking group well. Each week you walk not only to strengthen your body but to remember that your deeper strength comes from waiting on the Lord.

## Is it okay to walk on the Sabbath?

This is a question many people ask, and it deserves a careful answer. The Bible does not list walking as forbidden on the Sabbath, and the Gospels show Jesus and His disciples walking through grain fields on the Sabbath day (Mark 2:23). When the religious leaders objected, Jesus said, "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath" (Mark 2:27). He also taught that "it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days" (Matthew 12:12).

The Seventh-day Adventist Church's Fundamental Belief 20 describes the Sabbath as "a day of delightful communion with God and one another" and "the day of rest, worship, and ministry." A quiet walk in nature with family and friends fits naturally within that picture. Spending part of the afternoon in nature also fits a day that celebrates God as Creator, since the Sabbath points us back to the world He made and called very good.

The key is the spirit of the walk. Training for a race, chasing a personal record, or turning the afternoon into a hard workout would shift the focus toward ordinary weekday goals. A Sabbath walk is different. It is gentle, unhurried, and centered on gratitude, fellowship, and the beauty of what God has made. If you are unsure where the line is for you, read Isaiah 58:13 prayerfully and talk it over with your family or a pastor.

> "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." Psalm 19:1, KJV

Related: [Why Do Seventh-day Adventists Worship on Saturday?](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/why-do-seventh-day-adventists-worship-on-saturday/)

## How to start a Sabbath afternoon walking group

You do not need a committee or a budget to begin. A walking group can be as small as two friends or as large as a few families. What matters most is a simple plan, a welcoming spirit, and a little consistency.

- Invite : Ask two or three people after lunch
- Choose a route : Safe, well lit, and easy for everyone
- Set the pace : Walk at the speed of the slowest walker
- Add a moment of worship : A verse, a song, or a prayer
- Keep it going : Same time, same place, every week

### Start with a small circle

Begin by inviting a few people you already know, such as your family, a neighbor, or friends from church. Mayo Clinic suggests walking with a friend or neighbor or joining a walking group as a way to stay motivated. A small, faithful group often lasts longer than a large one that fizzles out.

### Pick a safe and pleasant route

Mayo Clinic advises walking in safe, well lit areas and avoiding the street or uneven, cracked sidewalks. For a Sabbath walk, look for a park, a quiet neighborhood, or a nature trail near where you live. Choose a loop that is easy to shorten, so that no one feels pressured to go farther than they can.

### Walk at the pace of the slowest walker

A Sabbath walk is not a race. Plan for the grandparent with a sore knee and the toddler who wants to look at every leaf. Harvard Health recommends warming up with five minutes of easy walking, and that fits a group perfectly. Let the first few minutes be slow and chatty, and let people who want a brisker pace walk a little ahead and circle back.

### Add a simple moment of worship

Before you start, read a short verse such as Psalm 19:1 or Isaiah 40:31 and say a brief prayer. Along the way, invite people to point out something in nature that reminds them of God's care. You might pause at the halfway point to share one thing each person is grateful for this week. These small habits keep the walk centered on the Lord of the Sabbath.

### Keep it simple and steady

Meet at the same time each week, perhaps right after the fellowship meal. Mayo Clinic encourages walkers to start with a small, achievable goal and to take missed days in stride, simply starting again when they can. If the group is ever tempted to grow into something more organized, check with your church leadership first so the effort can be planned and supported well.

## Practical tips for walking safely

Wear comfortable, supportive shoes that fit well. Harvard Health notes that sneakers are really all you need to get started, and Mayo Clinic recommends loose clothing suited to the weather. In North Texas, that usually means planning around the heat for much of the year, so bring water, choose shaded routes, and consider walking later in the afternoon when the sun is lower.

Mayo Clinic also suggests telling someone your route if you walk alone and wearing bright or reflective clothing if you will be out as it gets dark. Because the Sabbath ends at sunset, a late afternoon walk can finish with the sky turning gold, a beautiful time to close the day with prayer. If anyone in the group has heart disease, diabetes, joint problems, or another health condition, encourage them to talk with their doctor about what kind of activity is right for them.

## Walking together is a picture of the church

The Preacher in Ecclesiastes wrote, "Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up" (Ecclesiastes 4:9 to 10). Those words describe a walking group well, but they also describe the church. We were never meant to walk the Christian journey alone.

Think of the two disciples on the road to Emmaus after the crucifixion. Luke tells us that "while they communed together and reasoned, Jesus himself drew near, and went with them" (Luke 24:15). Some of the most meaningful conversations about faith happen side by side, on a path, with no rush to be anywhere else. Your Sabbath walk may become exactly that kind of place.

## Questions people ask

### How fast should I walk for it to count as exercise?

A walk counts as moderate exercise when it is brisk enough that your breathing speeds up but you can still talk in full sentences. Harvard Health calls this the talk test and suggests walking as if you are in a bit of a hurry. The CDC names brisk walking as an example of moderate intensity activity. That pace works well for a group, because everyone keeps moving while there is still room for conversation.

### Can I split my walking into shorter walks?

Yes, you can split your walking into shorter walks, because the CDC says you do not have to get all your activity at once. One simple way to reach the CDC goal of 150 minutes a week is to walk 30 minutes a day on five days a week. The Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans add that any amount of physical activity has some health benefits. A short walk after lunch counts, and so does every step you add from there.

### What do I need to start walking for exercise?

To start walking for exercise, all you really need is a pair of comfortable, supportive shoes that fit well. Harvard Health notes that sneakers are enough to get started, and Mayo Clinic recommends loose clothing suited to the weather. In North Texas, bring water and choose shaded routes during the hot months. If you have a health condition or have not been active for a while, check with your doctor before you begin.

### Is walking good for older adults?

Walking is very good for older adults, and Mayo Clinic says it can improve physical function and lower the risk of falls. Regular walking can also strengthen bones and muscles, lift mood, and improve sleep. For a group walk, warm up with five minutes of easy walking as Harvard Health recommends, and walk at the pace of the slowest walker. Anyone with heart disease, diabetes, joint problems, or another health condition should talk with their doctor about what kind of activity is right for them.

## Reflection questions

Consider these questions on your own or with the people you hope to walk with. Who in your life might be lonely on Sabbath afternoons and would be blessed by a simple invitation to walk? What would it look like for your family to spend part of the Sabbath enjoying creation instead of resting only indoors? How might walking alongside someone each week open the door to deeper conversations about faith?

## A word of encouragement

You do not have to be fit, organized, or outgoing to start something good. All it takes is one invitation and one afternoon. If only one other person says yes, that is a walking group.

As you walk, remember that the God who walked in the garden still delights in your company. He renews the strength of those who wait on Him, and He walks beside you on every path. Let each step be a small act of gratitude for the body, the friends, and the beautiful world He has given you.

## A prayer

Lord of the Sabbath, thank You for the gift of rest and for the beauty of everything You have made. Thank You for legs to walk, eyes to see Your handiwork, and friends to share the journey. Help us walk with You each day as Enoch did. Bless every step we take together, and draw near to us on the path just as You did on the road to Emmaus. Amen.

## Your next step

We would love to share a Sabbath with you. Join us on Saturday morning at 205 E Carver St in Alvarado, Texas, with Sabbath School at 10:00 AM and the Divine Service at 11:00 AM in Kreyòl and English, and stay for the meal our church family shares afterward. If a Sabbath afternoon walk sounds like something you would enjoy, the fellowship meal is a natural place to find a walking partner, so plan your first visit below.

# Diri ak Pwa the Healthy Way

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/diri-ak-pwa-the-healthy-way/
Category: Recipes
Author: Rose Charles
Published: 2026-08-31

A full recipe for Haitian rice and beans made with brown rice, dry beans, and homemade epis, with simple nutrition and Scripture for everyday meals.


There is a certain sound every Haitian kitchen knows: the soft hiss of epis hitting hot oil, followed by the smell of garlic, thyme, and clove filling the whole house. Someone lifts the lid on a pot of beans, pours that deep red cooking liquid over the rice, and everyone knows dinner will be good. For many families, diri ak pwa is not just a side dish. It is the taste of home, of Sunday dinners, of grandmothers who never measured anything.

Now imagine that your doctor has suggested more fiber and fewer refined carbohydrates, or that you simply want your family to eat a little better. Your first worry might be that you will have to give up the rice and beans you love. The truth is the opposite. With brown rice, beans cooked from dry, and a homemade epis, diri ak pwa can become one of the most nourishing meals on your table while still tasting the way it should.

In this article we will walk through a full recipe for healthy Haitian rice and beans, show you how to make a simple plant based epis, and explain why beans and whole grains are so good for you. Along the way we will look at what the Bible says about everyday meals.

## The short answer

Healthy diri ak pwa uses three simple upgrades: brown rice instead of white, beans cooked from dry so you control the salt, and fresh epis instead of salty bouillon cubes. The method is the same one Haitian cooks have always used. You cook the beans, save their flavorful liquid, fry the beans briefly with epis, then cook the rice right in that liquid until every grain is tinted and tender.

- 6 : Servings from one pot
- 1 cup : Dry beans, about 2 1/2 cups cooked
- 30 min : Minimum boil for kidney beans

The dish many Haitians call diri kole ak pwa, or rice cooked together with beans, is a beloved everyday dish across Haiti and its diaspora. The classic version is usually made with red kidney beans, though many cooks use pinto or other beans too. Our version keeps the classic flavors of thyme, clove, garlic, and a whole scotch bonnet pepper, and simply makes the grain a whole grain.

## Why beans and brown rice are good for you

### What makes brown rice different

Every grain of rice starts as a whole kernel with three parts. The Mayo Clinic describes them simply: the bran is the hard outer coating that holds most of the fiber, the germ contains vitamins and healthy fats, and the endosperm is the starchy center. Brown rice keeps all three parts. White rice has the bran and germ removed, and with them most of the fiber.

Harvard's Nutrition Source reports that refining grains strips away much of their fiber, B vitamins, and vitamin E. It also points to research linking higher white rice intake with a greater risk of type 2 diabetes, and two or more servings of brown rice a week with a lower risk. Studies like these show associations, not guarantees, but they give good reason to choose whole grains more often. The Mayo Clinic adds that whole grains may help lower insulin levels and the risk of diabetes and heart disease.

### What beans bring to the table

Beans are one of the most humble and powerful foods in the world. Harvard describes legumes as a source of protein, fiber, folate, and iron, and notes that whole legumes are low in saturated fat and sodium. The Mayo Clinic adds that legumes contain no cholesterol and provide potassium and magnesium, and that they can stand in for meat. The USDA's MyPlate counts beans in both the protein group and the vegetable group, which says a lot about how useful they are.

Together, beans and brown rice make a filling plate full of fiber and plant protein. Add a slice of avocado and a fresh salad, and you have a complete Haitian meal that fits the plant based eating many Adventists enjoy.

Related: [Eating for Life: Simple Plant Based Meals from Our Kitchen](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/eating-for-life-simple-plant-based-meals-from-our-kitchen/)

## What the Bible says about everyday meals

### Eating to the glory of God

Paul wrote to the believers in Corinth about food, conscience, and how Christians should live together. He closed the discussion with a sentence that turns every ordinary meal into something sacred.

> "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." 1 Corinthians 10:31, KJV

In context, Paul was talking about food offered to idols and about caring for the conscience of others. But the principle is clear and broad. Nothing is too ordinary to be offered to God, not even a pot of rice and beans on a Tuesday night.

### Daniel's simple plate

When Daniel and his friends were taken captive to Babylon, they were offered rich food from the king's table. Daniel asked for something simpler.

> "Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink." Daniel 1:12, KJV

The word "pulse" in the King James Version refers to food grown from seeds, which many Bible students understand to include vegetables, grains, and legumes. At the end of the trial, the Bible says, "at the end of ten days their countenances appeared fairer and fatter in flesh than all the children which did eat the portion of the king's meat" (Daniel 1:15). Scripture's main point is Daniel's faithfulness to God, not a diet plan, and we should be careful not to turn the story into a promise about weight or looks. Still, it is a beautiful picture of how simple foods, chosen with a faithful heart, were blessed by God.

## How to make a simple plant based epis

Epis is the flavor base of Haitian cooking, a blend of herbs, peppers, garlic, and onion that seasons everything from rice and beans to soups and stews. Many families keep a jar in the refrigerator at all times. Traditionally it is pounded by hand with a mortar and pestle, though most cooks today use a blender or food processor. This version makes about 1 1/2 cups.

| Epis ingredient | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Fresh parsley, stems and leaves | 1 packed cup |
| Scallions, roughly chopped | 4 |
| Green bell pepper, seeded and chopped | 1 medium |
| Small onion, chopped | 1 |
| Garlic | 8 cloves |
| Fresh thyme leaves | 1 tablespoon |
| Whole cloves | 2 |
| Fresh lime juice | 2 tablespoons |
| Olive oil | 1/3 cup |
| Scotch bonnet pepper, seeded | 1/4, optional |

Place everything in a blender or food processor and blend until you have a thick, bright green paste, scraping down the sides as needed. Add a tablespoon of water if it is too thick to move. Spoon it into a clean glass jar and refrigerate. Because homemade mixtures of fresh garlic and herbs in oil can carry a risk of botulism, Oregon State University Extension advises using them within 4 days, so freeze the rest in an ice cube tray and you will always have a few cubes ready for the next pot of beans.

## Diri ak pwa the healthy way: the recipe

This recipe serves 6. Plan to soak the beans overnight. Active time is about 30 minutes, cooking the beans takes about 1 hour to 1 1/2 hours, and the rice takes about 45 minutes plus a short rest.

| Ingredient | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Dry red kidney beans | 1 cup |
| Water for cooking the beans | 7 cups |
| Whole cloves | 4, divided |
| Long grain brown rice, rinsed | 2 cups |
| Olive oil | 2 tablespoons |
| Haitian epis | 1/3 cup |
| Garlic, minced | 3 cloves |
| Small onion, finely chopped | 1 |
| Fresh thyme | 4 sprigs |
| Whole scotch bonnet pepper | 1, left whole |
| Salt | 1 1/2 teaspoons, or to taste |
| Fresh parsley, chopped | 2 tablespoons, for serving |

- Soak : Soak the beans overnight, then rinse
- Boil : Cook beans until tender, saving the liquid
- Fry : Sauté epis, onion, garlic, and beans
- Simmer : Add rice, bean liquid, and herbs, then cover
- Rest : Let it steam 10 minutes, then fluff

### Step 1: Soak and cook the beans

Sort the beans, removing any shriveled ones or small stones, and rinse them well. Cover them with plenty of water and soak overnight in the refrigerator. The next day, drain and rinse the beans, then put them in a pot with 7 cups of fresh water and 2 of the cloves. Bring them to a full boil and keep them at a boil for at least 30 minutes, then lower the heat and simmer, partly covered, until the beans mash easily between your fingers. This usually takes 1 hour to 1 1/2 hours in total.

That boiling step matters. Raw or undercooked kidney beans contain a natural toxin, and Kansas State University food safety specialists advise boiling them in fresh water for at least 30 minutes and avoiding the slow cooker, which may not get hot enough. Wait to add salt until the rice step, because the Mayo Clinic notes that salt and acidic ingredients added early can toughen beans and slow their cooking.

### Step 2: Save the liquid and fry the beans

Strain the beans over a large bowl and save every drop of the cooking liquid, because it gives diri ak pwa its color and flavor. Measure the liquid and add water if needed to make 4 1/2 cups. In a heavy pot with a tight lid, warm the olive oil over medium heat and add the epis, onion, and garlic. Cook for 2 to 3 minutes until fragrant, then add the drained beans and stir for another 2 to 3 minutes so they soak up the seasoning.

### Step 3: Cook the rice

Add the rinsed brown rice and stir for a minute so every grain is coated. Pour in the 4 1/2 cups of bean liquid, then add the thyme, the remaining 2 cloves, the whole scotch bonnet, and the salt. Bring it to a boil and let it bubble uncovered for a few minutes, until the liquid drops just below the surface of the rice. Lower the heat as far as it will go, cover tightly, and cook for about 45 minutes without lifting the lid.

### Step 4: Rest and serve

Turn off the heat and let the pot rest, still covered, for 10 minutes so the rice finishes steaming. Remove the thyme stems, the cloves, and the scotch bonnet, and gently fluff the rice with a fork. Sprinkle with parsley and serve with sliced avocado, a green salad, steamed vegetables, or a spoonful of legim.

## Tips, substitutions, and storage

Brown rice can vary from brand to brand, so check it at 40 minutes. If the rice is still firm and the pot is dry, sprinkle in a quarter cup of hot water, cover, and cook a little longer. If you prefer the crispy layer at the bottom of the pot that many Haitians call graten, leave the pot on low for an extra few minutes, watching closely so it does not burn.

Pinto beans, black beans, or small red beans all work well in this recipe. If you are short on time, you can use two 15 ounce cans of beans, rinsed, and replace the bean liquid with low sodium vegetable broth, though the color will be lighter. Never use bouillon cubes without checking the label, since many contain animal products and a great deal of sodium.

**Keep it healthy and safe**
- Boil kidney beans hard for at least 30 minutes
- Add salt with the rice, not the beans
- Cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate
- Reheat leftovers to 165°F

Diri ak pwa keeps well in the refrigerator in a covered container for 3 to 4 days, and cooked beans freeze beautifully for later meals. Reheat leftovers until steaming hot, to 165°F as FoodSafety.gov recommends, adding a splash of water to loosen the rice. Making a big pot on Friday is a lovely way to prepare for the Sabbath, so your family can rest and still enjoy a warm, home cooked meal.

## Questions people ask

### Is Haitian rice and beans healthy?

Haitian rice and beans can be a very healthy meal when you use brown rice, beans cooked from dry, and fresh epis instead of salty bouillon cubes. Brown rice keeps the bran and germ, where most of the fiber lives, and Harvard's Nutrition Source links brown rice with a lower risk of type 2 diabetes. Beans add protein, fiber, folate, and iron while staying low in saturated fat and sodium. Together they make a filling plate of fiber and plant protein that fits the plant based eating many Seventh-day Adventists enjoy.

### What beans are used in diri ak pwa?

The classic diri ak pwa is usually made with red kidney beans, though many Haitian cooks use pinto or other beans too. Black beans and small red beans also work well in this recipe. If you use dry kidney beans, boil them in fresh water for at least 30 minutes, as Kansas State University food safety specialists advise, because raw or undercooked kidney beans contain a natural toxin. Save the cooking liquid, since it gives the rice its color and flavor.

### Can I use canned beans for diri ak pwa?

You can use canned beans for diri ak pwa when you are short on time, using two 15 ounce cans of beans, rinsed. Replace the bean cooking liquid with low sodium vegetable broth. The color of the rice will be lighter than the classic version made with beans cooked from dry. Check the label on any bouillon cubes before using them, since many contain animal products and a great deal of sodium.

### How long does diri ak pwa last in the fridge?

Diri ak pwa keeps well in a covered container in the refrigerator for 3 to 4 days. Cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate them, and cooked beans also freeze beautifully for later meals. When you reheat it, heat it until steaming hot, to 165°F as FoodSafety.gov recommends, adding a splash of water to loosen the rice. Making a big pot on Friday is a lovely way to prepare for the Sabbath.

## Reflection questions

Take a moment to think about these questions, on your own or with your family. Which everyday meal in your home could become a small act of worship if you offered it to God with gratitude? What might Daniel's quiet courage teach you about making faithful choices when everyone around you is doing something different? And who could you invite to share a plate of rice and beans this week?

## A word of encouragement

Healthy changes do not have to happen all at once. Maybe this week you try brown rice for the first time, and next month you make your own epis. Every small step taken with a willing heart honors the God who made you and loves you. The same Lord who blessed Daniel's simple meal is near to you at your own table, so cook with joy, eat with thanks, and trust Him with the rest.

## A prayer

Lord, thank You for daily bread and for the simple foods that grow from the earth. Thank You for the hands that taught us to cook and the families we gather with. Help us to eat, drink, and do everything for Your glory. Give us faithful hearts like Daniel's, and make every meal a reminder of Your goodness and care. In Jesus' name, Amen.

## Your next step

If you would like to learn more about the God who cares for every part of your life, we would be honored to study the Bible with you. Request a free Bible study and explore Scripture one on one, at your own pace. And if you live near Alvarado, come join us on a Saturday morning, when our church family worships in Kreyòl and English and shares a meal together after the Sabbath service.

- Source: [Whole Grains, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/what-should-you-eat/whole-grains/)

- Source: [Whole grains: Hearty options for a healthy diet, Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/nutrition-and-healthy-eating/in-depth/whole-grains/art-20047826)

- Source: [Legumes and Pulses, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/legumes-pulses/)

- Source: [Legumes: Protein rich foods, Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/nutrition-and-healthy-eating/in-depth/legumes/art-20044278)

- Source: [Protein Foods, USDA MyPlate](https://www.myplate.gov/eat-healthy/protein-foods)

- Source: [Cooking Dry Beans Safely, Kansas State University](https://www.k-state.edu/news/you-asked-it/articles/2017/10/cooking-dry-beans-safely.html)

- Source: [Safe Minimum Internal Temperatures, FoodSafety.gov](https://www.foodsafety.gov/food-safety-charts/safe-minimum-internal-temperatures)

- Source: [Herbs and Vegetables in Oil, Oregon State University Extension](https://extension.oregonstate.edu/node/154041)

> "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." 1 Corinthians 10:31, KJV

# Faith for the Journey: Lessons from Abraham

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/faith-for-the-journey-lessons-from-abraham/
Category: Devotional
Author: Hannah Price
Published: 2026-08-24

Abraham left home at 75 with only a promise, and his honest, imperfect journey shows how to trust God when you are starting over and cannot see the road ahead.


Picture the night before a big move. The suitcases are packed, the papers sit in a folder by the door, and the house already sounds different without the pictures on the walls. You know what you are leaving, but you only have a rough idea of what waits on the other side.

Many families know that feeling. Some left Haiti for a new country, a new language, and work that may not match the training they had back home. Others left a small town, a marriage, or a steady career, and some have never moved at all but stand at the edge of an uncertain next step.

The Bible has a story for people in that place. It belongs to an old man named Abram, later called Abraham, who left everything familiar because God spoke to him. His journey is not a polished success story, but it is honest and full of hope for anyone starting over.

## The short answer

The main lessons from Abraham's faith are that faith obeys before it sees the whole map, that God's promises take time, that God stays faithful even when we stumble, and that our true home is the city God is building. Hebrews 11:8 says Abraham "went out, not knowing whither he went." He trusted the One who called him more than his own plans.

> "By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went." Hebrews 11:8, KJV

That verse does not praise Abraham for being fearless or perfect. It praises him for trusting God enough to take the next step. The rest of his story in Genesis 12 through 25 shows what that trust looked like over a lifetime of tents, waiting, mistakes, and grace.

## What did God ask Abraham to leave behind?

God asked Abraham to leave his country, his relatives, and his father's household, which in the ancient world meant leaving behind the security of his extended family. Genesis 11:31 tells us the family had already moved from Ur of the Chaldees to Haran. Then the call came to go farther.

> "Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:" Genesis 12:1, KJV

God did not hand Abraham a map or a timeline, only a promise to bless "all families of the earth" through him (Genesis 12:3). The Bible says simply, "So Abram departed, as the LORD had spoken unto him," and adds that he "was seventy and five years old when he departed out of Haran" (Genesis 12:4). If you are starting over later in life, Abraham is good company.

- 75 : Abram's age when he left Haran
- 25 years : from leaving Haran to Isaac's birth
- 100 : Abraham's age when Isaac was born

## Abraham's journey, step by step

It helps to see Abraham's story as a long road rather than one dramatic moment. The highlights below follow the order Genesis gives them. Notice how much of the road is waiting.

- Genesis 12: The call: Abram leaves Haran at 75 and builds altars as he travels through Canaan

- Genesis 12:10 to 20: Fear in Egypt: During a famine he tells Pharaoh that Sarai is his sister

- Genesis 15: Counting the stars: God renews the promise and Abram believes Him

- Genesis 16: Trying to help God: Abram has a son, Ishmael, with Hagar, Sarai's servant

- Genesis 21: The promise kept: Isaac is born when Abraham is 100 years old

- Genesis 22: The hardest test: Abraham is asked to offer Isaac, and God provides a ram

Wherever Abram stopped, Genesis says he built an altar and "called upon the name of the LORD" (Genesis 12:8). The tent moved, but worship stayed. For anyone in transition, the address may change many times, yet the habit of meeting God can travel with you.

## Did Abraham ever doubt God?

Yes, the Bible honestly records moments when Abraham's fear and impatience got ahead of his faith. Scripture never hides these failures. That honesty is part of what makes his story so encouraging for ordinary people.

### Fear in Egypt

Soon after arriving in Canaan, a famine struck, and Abram went down to Egypt. Afraid the Egyptians would kill him to take his wife, he told Sarai, "Say, I pray thee, thou art my sister: that it may be well with me for thy sake" (Genesis 12:13). It was Pharaoh, not Abram, who asked the painful question, "What is this that thou hast done unto me?" (Genesis 12:18). Genesis 20 shows that Abraham repeated the same half truth years later.

### Running ahead of God

After ten years in Canaan with no child, Sarai suggested that Abram have a son through her servant Hagar, and "Abram hearkened to the voice of Sarai" (Genesis 16:2). The plan brought conflict and deep hurt, and Hagar fled into the wilderness, where God saw her and cared for her (Genesis 16:13). Genesis 16:16 notes that Abram was 86 when Ishmael was born, still fourteen years before Isaac would arrive.

**What Abraham's failures teach us**
- Faith and fear can live in the same heart
- Shortcuts often create new pain
- God does not cancel His promise when we stumble
- Honesty about our mistakes opens the door to grace

Many people who have moved or started over made choices under pressure that they would not make again. Abraham's story does not say those choices did not matter. It says God kept walking with him and kept His word.

## How was Abraham counted righteous?

Abraham was counted righteous because he believed God, not because he earned it with a perfect record. One clear night God told him to look up and count the stars, saying, "So shall thy seed be" (Genesis 15:5). Abraham took God at His word.

> "And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness." Genesis 15:6, KJV

Paul quotes this verse in Romans 4:3, and James 2:23 adds that Abraham "was called the Friend of God." The Seventh-day Adventist Church teaches the same truth in Fundamental Belief 10, The Experience of Salvation, which describes believers who "exercise faith in Jesus as Saviour and Lord, Substitute and Example." Abraham trusted a promise he could not yet see, and we trust the Savior that promise pointed to.

> "He staggered not at the promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God; And being fully persuaded that, what he had promised, he was able also to perform." Romans 4:20 to 21, KJV

Put Romans 4 next to Genesis 16 and you see something hopeful. The man who once ran ahead of God is remembered as someone who did not stagger. Faith is not a feeling we either have or lack, but a relationship that grows as God proves Himself faithful.

## What is the lesson of Abraham and Isaac?

The lesson of Abraham and Isaac is that God can be trusted with the thing we love most, and that God Himself provides the sacrifice. In Genesis 22 God tested Abraham by asking him to offer Isaac, the son of promise, on a mountain in the land of Moriah. God stopped Abraham before any harm came to Isaac and provided a ram instead, and elsewhere Scripture plainly calls child sacrifice an abomination that the LORD hates (Deuteronomy 12:31).

> "And Abraham said, My son, God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering: so they went both of them together." Genesis 22:8, KJV

Hebrews 11:17 to 19 tells us what was happening in Abraham's heart: he was "accounting that God was able to raise him up, even from the dead." That is why he told his servants, "I and the lad will go yonder and worship, and come again to you" (Genesis 22:5). Many Christians, including Seventh-day Adventists, understand this story as a picture of the Father who did not hold back His own Son, Jesus, the Lamb God truly provided.

## Living in tents, looking for a city

Abraham never owned much of the land God promised him. When Sarah died, he told the local people, "I am a stranger and a sojourner with you" (Genesis 23:4). Hebrews explains how he could live that way without losing hope.

> "For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God." Hebrews 11:10, KJV

Hebrews 11:13 says Abraham and his family "died in faith, not having received the promises," confessing "that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth." That is a tender word for anyone caught between two places, not fully at home in the old country or the new one. Our deepest belonging is in the "better country" God has prepared (Hebrews 11:16), and that hope can steady us while we build a life here.

## Questions people ask about Abraham's faith

### What does Hebrews 11:8 mean?

Hebrews 11:8 means that Abraham obeyed God's call before he knew where it would lead, trusting God's character more than his own understanding. The verse moves in order: God called, Abraham obeyed, and he went out "not knowing whither he went." It teaches that faith often begins with one obedient step rather than a complete plan.

### Is it wrong to leave home to start a new life?

The Bible does not treat leaving home as wrong in itself, and Abraham left at God's direction. Scripture is full of people who moved because of famine, danger, family loyalty, or God's call, including Jacob, Naomi, and Ruth. What matters most is seeking God in the decision and keeping worship at the center wherever you settle.

### How do I trust God when I cannot see the next step?

You trust God in uncertainty by taking the next faithful step He has shown you while remembering how He has already kept His word. Abraham built altars as reminders, prayed, and waited, and he still made mistakes along the way. Reading God's promises, praying with others, and staying close to a church family can help your faith grow the way his did.

## Walking by faith this week

Abraham's lessons fit the very real decisions in front of us, whether you are new to this country, new to this town, or facing a door you did not expect. Here is a simple way to carry them into the coming days. Choose one step and begin today.

- Build an altar : Set a daily time and place to pray, even in a temporary home
- Name the promise : Write down one promise of God and read it each morning
- Take one step : Do the next faithful thing instead of solving the whole future
- Refuse shortcuts : Bring pressure to God before reaching for a quick fix
- Share the road : Tell a trusted believer what you face and pray together

Haitian families have a proverb that fits Abraham well: "Piti piti zwazo fè nich li," little by little the bird builds its nest. Rebuilding a life rarely happens all at once. It happens one friendship, one Sabbath, and one prayer at a time, with God walking beside you.

Related: [Resting in His Presence: What the Sabbath Teaches Us About Trust](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/resting-in-his-presence-what-the-sabbath-teaches-us-about-trust/)

## Reflection questions

Take a few quiet minutes with these questions, alone or with someone you trust. Where is God asking you to take a next step without seeing the whole road, and what makes that step hard? Which part of Abraham's story, his obedience, his failures, or his long wait, feels most like your season right now? What daily habit could help you remember God's faithfulness while life is still unsettled?

## A word of encouragement

If you have left a lot behind, God sees every goodbye you said and every tear you hid. The same God who called Abraham by name knows your name and the city you are really traveling toward. Your mistakes along the way do not cancel His promises, any more than Abraham's did. Keep walking, keep praying, and trust that what He has promised, He is able also to perform.

## A prayer

Faithful God, thank You for walking with Abraham through every tent, famine, and long night of waiting. Some of us are far from the places we once called home, and some of us stand at a door we do not understand. Give us faith to take the next step You show us, honesty to bring You our fears, and hope in the city whose builder and maker is You. We ask in the name of Jesus, the Lamb You provided. Amen.

## Your next step

If you are in a season of change and would like someone to pray with you, our church family would be honored to do that. You can send a prayer request and share as much or as little as you are comfortable sharing. We would also love to welcome you at Shekinah Haitian Seventh-day Adventist Church in Alvarado, Texas, where we worship in Kreyòl and English, with Sabbath School at 10:00 AM and Divine Service at 11:00 AM on Saturday, followed by a meal together. Wherever your journey started, there is a place for you at our table.

- Source: [Genesis Chapter 12 (King James Bible Online)](https://www.kingjamesbibleonline.org/Genesis-Chapter-12/)

- Source: [Genesis Chapter 22 (King James Bible Online)](https://www.kingjamesbibleonline.org/Genesis-Chapter-22/)

- Source: [Romans Chapter 4 (King James Bible Online)](https://www.kingjamesbibleonline.org/Romans-Chapter-4/)

- Source: [Hebrews Chapter 11 (King James Bible Online)](https://www.kingjamesbibleonline.org/Hebrews-Chapter-11/)

- Source: [Fundamental Belief 10: The Experience of Salvation (Seventh-day Adventist Church)](https://adventist.org/beliefs/official/experience-of-salvation)

- Source: [Why Was Abraham Tested by God? (Christianity.com)](https://www.christianity.com/wiki/bible/why-was-abraham-tested-by-god.html)

> "By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went." Hebrews 11:8, KJV

# Water First: Small Habits for Big Energy

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/water-first-small-habits-for-big-energy/
Category: Health
Author: Michael Reed
Published: 2026-08-17

Simple water habits support the body God made, and every glass can remind us of the living water Jesus offers to all who are thirsty.


It is three in the afternoon, and the familiar slump arrives right on schedule. Your eyes feel heavy, your focus drifts, and you start thinking about a sugary soda or a snack from the vending machine. Then you realize you have not had anything to drink since breakfast. It is a small thing, easy to overlook in a busy day, and yet it is one of the simplest habits we can change.

Water is so ordinary that we rarely think about it as a gift. It comes out of the tap whenever we need it. Yet Scripture treats water as something precious, a sign of God's provision in the wilderness and a picture of the eternal life that Jesus offers to everyone who is thirsty.

In this article we will look at what trusted health sources say about how much water adults need, the common signs that you may need more fluid, and some practical habits for drinking water through the day. We will also look at what the Bible means when it speaks of living water. This is general health education rather than medical advice, so if you have a health condition that affects fluids, such as heart or kidney disease, follow your doctor's guidance.

## The short answer

- 3.7 liters : Average daily total water for adequately hydrated men (National Academies)
- 2.7 liters : Average daily total water for adequately hydrated women
- 20% : Share of total water that typically comes from food

There is no single number that fits everyone. In its 2004 report on water and electrolytes, the National Academies found that women who appear adequately hydrated take in an average of about 2.7 liters, or 91 ounces, of total water a day, and men about 3.7 liters, or 125 ounces. That total includes water from all drinks and from food, not only plain water.

The same report gives encouraging news. It says the vast majority of healthy people adequately meet their daily hydration needs by letting thirst be their guide. So the goal is not to force down a certain number of glasses, but to build simple habits that make water easy and natural, while paying attention to times when your body needs more.

## How much water should I drink a day?

Many people have heard the rule of eight glasses a day. Mayo Clinic calls it easy to remember and a good goal, while noting that some people need less fluid and others need more. Mayo also points to studies suggesting that the average healthy adult gets enough water with about 11.5 to 15.5 cups of total fluid a day, roughly 2.7 to 3.7 liters, which matches the National Academies figures.

It helps to remember that these numbers describe total water. The National Academies report says that about 80 percent of total water comes from drinks of all kinds, and about 20 percent comes from food. Fruits, vegetables, soups, and cooked grains all contribute. A plant based diet rich in produce naturally adds water to your day.

| What affects your water needs | Why it matters (Mayo Clinic) |
| --- | --- |
| Exercise | Sweating means you need extra fluid to cover the loss |
| Hot or humid weather | You sweat more and need more water |
| Illness | Fever, vomiting, or diarrhea cause fluid loss |
| Pregnancy and breastfeeding | The body needs extra fluid in these seasons |
| Health conditions | Some conditions, such as bladder infections or kidney stones, raise fluid needs |

For those of us in North Texas, the heat is a real factor for much of the year. Working outdoors, mowing the yard, or watching a game in the sun all increase the water your body loses. On those days, keep water within reach.

## How do I know if I am drinking enough?

Mayo Clinic offers two simple signs that you are probably getting enough fluid. You rarely feel thirsty, and your urine is colorless or light yellow. Those two checks are often more useful than counting cups, because they reflect what your own body needs on that particular day.

### Signs of dehydration in adults

When the body does not have enough fluid, it begins to send signals. Mayo Clinic lists common signs of dehydration in adults, including strong thirst, urinating less often than usual, dark colored urine, fatigue, dizziness, and confusion. The CDC adds that dehydration can lead to unclear thinking, mood changes, overheating, constipation, and kidney stones.

**Common signs of dehydration (Mayo Clinic)**
- Strong thirst
- Urinating less than usual
- Dark colored urine
- Fatigue
- Dizziness
- Confusion

### A special word about older adults

Mayo Clinic notes that thirst is not always a reliable signal, especially for older adults, who may not feel thirsty until they are already dehydrated. As we age, the body's fluid reserve becomes smaller, and conditions such as diabetes, certain medicines, or difficulty getting water independently can raise the risk. If you care for an aging parent or grandparent, offering water regularly throughout the day is a simple act of love.

### When to call a doctor

Mayo Clinic advises contacting a health care professional if you or a loved one has had diarrhea for 24 hours or longer or cannot keep fluids down. The same applies to someone who seems confused or unusually sleepy, has bloody or black stool, or has a fever of 102 degrees or higher. These are signs that the body needs more help than a glass of water can give.

It is also possible, though rare, to drink too much. Mayo Clinic explains that drinking far too much water can lower sodium in the blood to a dangerous level, a condition called hyponatremia, which can be life threatening. This is uncommon in healthy adults but can happen to some athletes when they prepare for a long or intense workout. More is not always better, and listening to your body matters here too.

## What water does for your body

Water is involved in nearly everything your body does. Mayo Clinic explains that cells, tissues, and organs need water to work as they should. Water helps the body manage its temperature through sweating, maintain fluid balance in and around cells, make body fluids such as tears and urine, support digestion, and remove waste.

The CDC adds another practical benefit. Because plain water has no calories, choosing it instead of sugary drinks can help reduce the calories you take in. The CDC notes that regular sodas, fruit drinks, sports drinks, energy drinks, and sweetened teas contain calories but little nutritional value. Swapping even one sugary drink a day for water is a meaningful step.

### Is drinking water first thing in the morning really better?

You may have seen claims that drinking water on an empty stomach in the morning detoxifies the body or burns fat. We could not find credible health sources that support those dramatic promises, so we do not repeat them here. What is true is simpler and still valuable. You go many hours overnight without drinking, and a glass of water when you wake up is an easy, natural way to start the day well. Placing that first glass next to your morning devotions can turn a health habit into a spiritual one.

## Small habits for drinking more water

Good habits work best when they are simple. The CDC offers several practical ideas that fit almost any lifestyle. Each of them is easy to try this week.

- Morning glass : Drink water when you wake, before anything else
- Carry a bottle : Keep a reusable bottle with you all day
- Water with meals : Serve water at the table for the whole family
- Swap one drink : Replace one sugary drink with water
- Add flavor naturally : Try a slice of lemon or lime

The CDC suggests carrying a reusable water bottle, freezing some water in freezer safe bottles so you have cold water all day, choosing water over sugary drinks, ordering water when you eat out, and serving water during meals. It also recommends adding a wedge of lemon or lime for a little flavor. For many Haitian families, a squeeze of fresh lime is already a familiar taste, and it can make a pitcher of cold water feel like a treat on a hot afternoon.

## Water in the Adventist health message

Seventh-day Adventists believe that caring for the body is part of faithful living. Paul wrote, "Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God" (1 Corinthians 10:31). The church's Fundamental Belief 22, Christian Behavior, encourages believers to care for their health through practices such as exercise, rest, and a healthful diet, as part of living in harmony with biblical principles.

Many Adventist churches teach eight natural remedies for health: good nutrition, exercise, water, sunlight, temperance, fresh air, rest, and trust in God. Water has its own place on that list, a reminder that some of God's best gifts for our health are simple and freely available. The apostle John expressed this kind of whole person care when he wrote, "Beloved, I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospereth" (3 John 1:2).

Related: [The Gift of Rest: Why Sleep Is Part of Our Worship](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/the-gift-of-rest-why-sleep-is-part-of-our-worship/)

## Living water: what the Bible means

Water appears throughout Scripture, from the rivers of Eden to the river of life in the new earth. It often stands for life and God's provision. The psalmist used thirst to describe the deepest longing of the human heart.

> "As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God. My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God?" Psalm 42:1 to 2, KJV

Just as a deer in a dry land searches for a stream, the soul searches for God. Our bodies remind us every day that we are not self sufficient. We need water from outside ourselves to live. In the same way, our souls need the life that only God can give.

### Jesus at the well

In John 4, Jesus sat by a well in Samaria about the sixth hour, tired from His journey, and asked a woman for a drink. Their conversation moved quickly from the water in the well to the water He came to give. Jesus told her, "Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again" (John 4:13), and then He offered something far greater.

> "But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life." John 4:14, KJV

Jesus was not dismissing physical water. He was using it to point to a deeper need. He offered her a gift that would meet her thirst from the inside out.

### An invitation to anyone who is thirsty

Later, at the Feast of Tabernacles in Jerusalem, Jesus made the invitation public. John records that on "the last day, that great day of the feast, Jesus stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink. He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water" (John 7:37 to 38). In the next verse John explains that Jesus was speaking of the Spirit, whom believers would receive (John 7:39).

That invitation echoes a much older one from the prophet Isaiah, who wrote, "Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price" (Isaiah 55:1). God's grace has never been for sale. It is offered freely to anyone who will come.

The Bible closes with the same welcome. "And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely" (Revelation 22:17). From beginning to end, Scripture uses water to show us a generous God who satisfies the thirsty.

## Making water a daily reminder of grace

Here is a simple idea that brings the body and the spirit together. Each morning, as you pour your first glass of water, let it remind you of the living water Jesus offers. You might pray a short sentence such as, "Lord, as this water refreshes my body, let Your Spirit refresh my soul today." Over time, a small physical habit can become a daily doorway into prayer.

Families can do this together too. Before a meal, as glasses are filled, a parent might read one of the verses from this article. Children will remember Jesus at the well far longer than a lecture about hydration, and parents who reach for water themselves teach by example.

## Questions people ask

### Do food and other drinks count toward daily water intake?

Yes, food and other drinks count toward your daily water intake, because the recommended amounts describe total water from all sources. The National Academies report found that about 80 percent of total water comes from drinks of all kinds and about 20 percent comes from food. Fruits, vegetables, soups, and cooked grains all contribute. A plant based diet rich in produce naturally adds water to your day.

### Is thirst a good guide for how much water to drink?

For most healthy people, thirst is a good guide, since the National Academies report says the vast majority meet their daily hydration needs by letting thirst be their guide. Mayo Clinic adds that if you rarely feel thirsty and your urine is colorless or light yellow, you are probably getting enough fluid. Thirst is not always reliable for older adults, who may not feel thirsty until they are already dehydrated. If you care for an aging parent or grandparent, offering water regularly through the day is a simple act of love.

### Can you drink too much water?

Yes, it is possible to drink too much water, though it is rare in healthy adults. Mayo Clinic explains that drinking far too much water can lower sodium in the blood to a dangerous level, a condition called hyponatremia, which can be life threatening. It can happen to some athletes when they prepare for a long or intense workout. More is not always better, so listen to your body and follow your doctor's guidance if you have a condition that affects fluids.

### Why is water better than sugary drinks?

Water is better than sugary drinks because plain water has no calories, so choosing it can help reduce the calories you take in. The CDC notes that regular sodas, fruit drinks, sports drinks, energy drinks, and sweetened teas contain calories but little nutritional value. Swapping even one sugary drink a day for water is a meaningful step. For a little flavor, the CDC suggests adding a wedge of lemon or lime, a taste many Haitian families already love.

## Reflection questions

Take a moment to think about these questions, perhaps with a glass of water in hand. What tends to crowd water out of your day, and what one small change could make it easier to choose? In what areas of your life have you been trying to satisfy a deeper thirst with things that leave you thirsty again? How might Jesus' words at the well invite you to come to Him today, just as you are?

## A word of encouragement

You do not have to overhaul your whole life to take better care of your body. Start with one glass of water in the morning or one sugary drink replaced at lunch. Small, steady habits add up, and God is patient with us as we grow.

The same is true of your spiritual life. Jesus did not ask the woman at the well to fix everything before He offered her living water. He simply invited her to receive. Whatever you are carrying today, that invitation is open to you as well, and His supply never runs dry.

## A prayer

Lord Jesus, thank You for the simple gift of clean water and for the body You have given me. Help me care for it with wisdom and gratitude. Most of all, thank You for the living water of Your Spirit. When my soul feels dry and weary, draw me to You again, and let Your life spring up in me today and forever. Amen.

## Your next step

If the story of Jesus at the well stirred something in you, we would love to help you explore it further. You can request a free Bible study below and read through the Gospel of John one on one, at your own pace, with someone from Shekinah who would be glad to walk with you. You are also welcome to join us any Sabbath at 205 E Carver St in Alvarado, Texas.

- Source: [Report Sets Dietary Intake Levels for Water, Salt, and Potassium, National Academies](https://www.nationalacademies.org/news/report-sets-dietary-intake-levels-for-water-salt-and-potassium-to-maintain-health-and-reduce-chronic-disease-risk)

- Source: [Water: How much should you drink every day? Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/nutrition-and-healthy-eating/in-depth/water/art-20044256)

- Source: [Dehydration: Symptoms and causes, Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/dehydration/symptoms-causes/syc-20354086)

- Source: [About Water and Healthier Drinks, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-weight-growth/water-healthy-drinks/index.html)

- Source: [Fundamental Belief 22: Christian Behavior, Seventh-day Adventist Church](https://www.adventist.org/beliefs/official/christian-behavior/)

> "But whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life." John 4:14, KJV

# Legim Without Meat: A Family Favorite

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/legim-without-meat-a-family-favorite/
Category: Recipes
Author: Sophia Bennett
Published: 2026-08-10

Make a rich, fully plant based Haitian legim with eggplant, cabbage, carrots, chayote, and epis, then learn what to serve with it and how to store it safely.


Imagine a Friday afternoon with the Sabbath only a few hours away. You want a meal that can rest quietly on the stove, feed the whole family, and still taste wonderful when you warm it up after church the next day. Maybe you grew up with a big pot of legim simmering in your mother's kitchen, but you remember it cooked with beef or crab, and you are not sure how to make it without meat. Or maybe a Haitian friend served you a plate of legim over rice and you have been thinking about it ever since.

Whatever brought you here, this pot is for you. Legim is one of those dishes that teaches patience, because the vegetables need time to soften, blend, and become something richer than they were on their own. The good news is that the deep, comforting flavor of legim comes mostly from the vegetables and the seasoning, not from the meat.

In this article we share an original, fully plant based Haitian legim recipe, with an option to add chickpeas or beans for protein. We also answer the questions people ask most, like what to serve with legim and how long it keeps, using guidance from FoodSafety.gov and the USDA. Along the way we will look at one short proverb that has a lot to say about what makes a meal truly good.

## The short answer

Haitian legim is a thick vegetable stew of eggplant, cabbage, carrots, and chayote cooked down with onion, garlic, epis, tomato paste, and thyme, then partly mashed and finished with spinach or watercress. To make legim without meat, build flavor with a generous amount of epis, let the tomato paste darken in the oil, and add chickpeas or beans for protein. Serve it over rice.

- 25 min : Prep time
- 1 hour : Cook time
- 6 servings : Makes

## What is Haitian legim?

Legim is a hearty Haitian stew in which the vegetables are cooked until very soft and then mashed partway, so the pot becomes thick, glossy, and spoonable. Legim is the Haitian Creole spelling, while many English recipes use the French word légume, which is why you will also see it written as Haitian legume. Haitian chef Sabine Mondesir, writing for Life and Thyme, describes legume as one of the most popular dishes served in Haitian restaurants and notes that it is usually made with stewed beef or goat, sometimes pork, and with seafood such as crab for special occasions. She also observes that no two mothers or grandmothers seem to share the same recipe, and that is part of the joy of this dish.

Mondesir describes legume as a mashed stew of eggplant, cabbage, chayote, spinach, watercress, and other vegetables, depending on the household, and many cooks add carrots as well. Chayote is the pale green squash that cooks in Louisiana call mirliton. The vegetables are seasoned with epis, which she describes as a marinade or paste of green onions, thyme, parsley, peppers, and garlic. Because the vegetables carry so much of the flavor, legim adapts beautifully to a plant based kitchen.

### A plant based legim for Adventist kitchens

For Seventh-day Adventist families, a meatless legim fits naturally with the way many of us already cook. Fundamental Belief 22 of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, on Christian Behavior, encourages us to care for our bodies intelligently and to "adopt the most healthful diet possible." The Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health Nutrition Source reports that a diet rich in vegetables and fruits can lower blood pressure and reduce the risk of heart disease and stroke. A single pot of legim holds at least five different vegetables, which makes it an easy way to put that counsel on the table.

## The recipe: Shekinah style legim without meat

This is our own family style version, written to be forgiving and simple. You will need a large, heavy pot with a lid, a sharp knife, and a potato masher or a sturdy wooden spoon. If you do not have homemade epis, a good store bought Haitian epis works, though you may need less salt, so taste before seasoning. Cut the vegetables into roughly even pieces so they soften at the same pace.

| Ingredient | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Olive oil or other vegetable oil | 2 tablespoons |
| Yellow onion, chopped | 1 large |
| Garlic cloves, minced | 4 |
| Haitian epis, homemade or store bought | 1/3 cup |
| Tomato paste | 3 tablespoons |
| Eggplant, cut into 1 inch cubes | 1 large, about 1 1/2 pounds |
| Green cabbage, cored and chopped | 1/2 small head, about 4 cups |
| Carrots, sliced into rounds | 3 medium |
| Chayote (mirliton), peeled and cubed | 2 medium |
| Green bell pepper, chopped | 1 |
| Fresh thyme | 4 sprigs, or 1 teaspoon dried |
| Whole cloves | 3 |
| Low sodium vegetable broth or water | 1 1/2 cups |
| Fresh spinach or watercress, roughly chopped | 5 ounces, about 5 packed cups |
| Cooked chickpeas or red kidney beans, drained and rinsed (optional) | 1 1/2 cups, or one 15 ounce can |
| Whole scotch bonnet pepper (optional) | 1 |
| Fresh lime juice | 1 lime |
| Salt and black pepper | To taste |

- Build the base : Cook onion, garlic, and epis in the oil for about 5 minutes
- Darken the paste : Stir in tomato paste and cook 2 minutes until it turns deeper red
- Add vegetables : Add eggplant, cabbage, carrots, chayote, bell pepper, thyme, cloves, and broth
- Simmer : Cover and cook gently 35 to 40 minutes until everything is very tender
- Mash and finish : Remove pepper, thyme stems, and cloves, mash partway, then add greens, beans, and lime

### How do you make legim without meat?

You make legim without meat by letting the seasoning do the work that the meat usually does. Start by warming the oil over medium heat and cooking the onion, garlic, and epis for about five minutes, stirring often, until the kitchen smells fragrant and the onion is soft. Stir in the tomato paste and keep it moving for two minutes, until it darkens a shade and clings to the bottom of the pot. That little bit of browning gives the stew a savory depth that keeps anyone from missing the meat.

Next add the eggplant, cabbage, carrots, chayote, bell pepper, thyme, and cloves, along with the broth and a teaspoon of salt. If you want gentle heat, lay the scotch bonnet on top whole and unbroken, so it perfumes the pot without bursting. Cover and let everything simmer over low to medium heat for 35 to 40 minutes, stirring every ten minutes or so and adding a splash of water if the bottom looks dry. The stew is ready to mash when a carrot slice breaks easily against the side of the pot.

Carefully lift out the scotch bonnet, the thyme stems, and as many cloves as you can find. Mash about half of the vegetables right in the pot, leaving some pieces whole so the legim has both creaminess and texture. Stir in the spinach or watercress and the chickpeas or beans, cover, and cook ten minutes more. Finish with the lime juice, then taste and adjust the salt and black pepper before serving.

### A few kitchen notes

If you rinse canned chickpeas or beans, you also lower the salt in the finished pot. The Harvard Nutrition Source notes that draining and rinsing canned chickpeas removes about 40 percent of the sodium. If you cannot find chayote, a small zucchini added during the last 15 minutes of simmering makes a reasonable stand in. And if you ever slice a scotch bonnet instead of leaving it whole, wear gloves and keep your hands away from your eyes.

Related: [Diri ak Pwa the Healthy Way](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/diri-ak-pwa-the-healthy-way/)

For a simple homemade epis to use in this legim, the recipe in our diri ak pwa article walks you through it step by step. Making your own means you control exactly how much salt goes into your food. It also lets you season the pot the way your family likes it best.

## Questions people ask

### What do you serve with legim?

Legim is traditionally served with white rice and a spoonful of pikliz, the spicy pickled cabbage and scotch bonnet condiment, as Haitian chef Sabine Mondesir describes for Life and Thyme. It is just as good over brown rice or beside a plate of diri ak pwa. The crunch and heat of the pikliz balance the soft, savory stew. For a complete plant based plate, add the chickpeas or beans to the pot and serve with a whole grain and a fresh salad.

### How long does legim last in the fridge?

Cooked legim keeps in the refrigerator for 3 to 4 days, according to FoodSafety.gov, as long as you refrigerate it within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour if the food is sitting somewhere hotter than 90°F. Because legim is a big, dense pot, the USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service recommends dividing large amounts of food into shallow containers so they cool quickly. Do not leave the whole pot on the stove to cool overnight. Legim also freezes well, and the USDA says leftovers can be frozen for 3 to 4 months, then thawed safely in the refrigerator, in cold water, or in the microwave.

### How do you reheat legim safely?

Reheat legim until it reaches 165°F on a food thermometer, which is the reheating temperature FoodSafety.gov gives for leftovers. The USDA also advises reheating soups and sauces by bringing them to a rolling boil, so a thick stew like legim should be warmed on the stove over medium heat with a splash of water until it bubbles throughout. Warm only what you plan to eat, and return the rest to the refrigerator promptly.

**Legim food safety at a glance**
- Refrigerate within 2 hours of cooking, or 1 hour above 90°F
- Cool large batches in shallow containers
- Eat refrigerated legim within 3 to 4 days
- Freeze for 3 to 4 months
- Reheat to 165°F, bringing the stew to a boil

## Good food for the body God gave us

Legim is a quiet nutritional gift. The Harvard Nutrition Source encourages eating a variety of types and colors of produce to give your body the mix of nutrients it needs, and this pot holds purple eggplant, orange carrots, pale green chayote, and dark leafy greens all at once. Harvard also names green leafy vegetables, such as spinach, as the group most closely tied to lower risk of cardiovascular disease.

Fiber is another reason to love this dish. According to the Harvard Nutrition Source, adults need at least 25 to 35 grams of fiber a day, yet most Americans get only about 15 grams. Harvard lists vegetables and legumes such as beans and chickpeas among the great sources of fiber, which helps keep hunger and blood sugar in check and is linked with a lower risk of heart disease. Adding chickpeas or beans to legim also brings plant protein to the plate, turning a side dish into a satisfying main meal.

## A dinner of herbs where love is

The Bible reminds us that from the very beginning God gave people the plants of the earth as food. "And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat" (Genesis 1:29, KJV). In the language of the King James Version, "meat" simply means food. A pot of legim is a humble reminder of that original, generous provision.

Solomon adds a lesson that goes deeper than ingredients. In the King James Version, the word "herbs" points to a plain meal of greens and vegetables, and a "stalled ox" is a fattened animal prepared for a feast. Put side by side, the two meals could hardly be more different.

> "Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith." Proverbs 15:17, KJV

The proverb does not tell us that a vegetable dinner is holy and a feast is sinful. It teaches that the love around the table matters more than how rich the food is. A simple pot of legim shared with patience, laughter, and prayer can be a richer meal than the finest banquet eaten in anger.

## Reflection questions

Who in your life could you invite to share a simple meal this week, and what might that invitation mean to them? When you sit down to eat with your family, what helps your table feel like a place where love is present? How might cooking more plant based meals become a way of thanking God for the body and the food He has given you?

## A word of encouragement

You do not need a perfect kitchen or an expensive grocery list to serve a meal that blesses people. A pot of vegetables, some seasoning, and a heart that wants to love others are enough. God sees the care you put into feeding your family, even on the days when it feels ordinary. Let every stirring of the pot be a small act of worship and gratitude.

## A prayer

Lord, thank You for the vegetables of the field, for the hands that grow them, and for the table where we gather. Fill our homes with the kind of love that makes the simplest meal a feast. Help us care for the bodies You have given us and open our doors to those who need a seat at the table. In Jesus' name, amen.

## Your next step

If you love Haitian food and warm fellowship, we would be glad to share a meal with you. At Shekinah Haitian Seventh-day Adventist Church in Alvarado, Texas, our church family shares a meal together after the Sabbath service. Join us at 205 E Carver St for Sabbath School at 10:00 AM and the Divine Service at 11:00 AM, with worship in Kreyòl and English. Plan your visit this Sabbath and come hungry, both for good food and for the Word of God.

- Source: [Leftovers and Food Safety, USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service](https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/leftovers-and-food-safety)

- Source: [Vegetables and Fruits, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health Nutrition Source](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/what-should-you-eat/vegetables-and-fruits/)

- Source: [Fiber, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health Nutrition Source](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/carbohydrates/fiber/)

- Source: [Chickpeas (Garbanzo Beans), Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health Nutrition Source](https://nutritionsource.hsph.harvard.edu/food-features/chickpeas-garbanzo-beans/)
