# Stress Less: Trusting God With Your Worries

URL: https://shekinahsda.org/blog/stress-less-trusting-god-with-your-worries/
Category: Health
Author: Nathan Hughes
Published: 2026-08-03

Learn how to manage everyday stress with practical habits backed by trusted health sources and the comfort of Bible promises about bringing every worry to God.


It is late, the house is quiet, and your mind will not slow down as you think about the bills, a distant child, or an uneasy phone call from family. Your shoulders are tight, your stomach is unsettled, and sleep feels far away. If that sounds familiar, you are not weak and you are not alone.

Stress is part of life in a broken world, and Scripture never pretends otherwise. Jesus spoke tenderly to people who were worried about food, clothing, and tomorrow. God also gave us bodies that respond to how we eat, move, rest, and breathe.

This article brings both together. We will look at what health experts say about stress and practical habits that help, and then we will open the Bible to hear what God says about worry. This is general wellness education, not medical advice, so please talk with your doctor or a licensed counselor about your own situation.

## The short answer

To manage stress, start with the basics the Mayo Clinic and the National Institute of Mental Health recommend: regular exercise, enough sleep, healthy meals, slow breathing or other relaxation practices, and honest conversation with people who support you. These habits help calm the body's stress response. The Bible adds an invitation to bring every worry to God in prayer, because He cares for you, as 1 Peter 5:7 promises.

- 7+ hours : Nightly sleep the CDC advises for adults 18 to 60
- 150 min : Weekly moderate activity the CDC advises for adults
- 988 : Call or text in a crisis (NIMH)

Faith and good habits are not rivals. Prayer does not replace a doctor, and a doctor does not replace prayer. If stress feels constant, keeps you from daily life, or comes with thoughts of hurting yourself, the National Institute of Mental Health says it may be time to talk to a professional, and in a crisis you can call or text 988 right away.

## What is stress, and when does it become a problem?

The National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) describes stress as the physical or mental response to an external cause, such as a heavy workload or an illness. Stress is not always bad, since it can push you to meet a deadline or prepare for something important. NIMH also explains that a stressor may be a one time event or something that happens again and again over a long time. The trouble comes when the pressure never lets up and your body never gets the signal that it is safe to rest.

### What are the signs of chronic stress?

Common signs of ongoing stress include constant worry, tension, headaches or body pain, trouble sleeping, and feeling uneasy most of the time. The NIMH fact sheet "I'm So Stressed Out!" says stress may be a concern when its symptoms interfere with everyday life, cause you to avoid doing things, or seem to be always present. It also lists high blood pressure and loss of sleep among the possible effects. NIMH notes that anxiety is the body's reaction to stress and can show up even when there is no current threat.

**Signs worth taking seriously**
- Worry that seems always present
- Avoiding people or tasks because of stress
- Headaches, body pain, or tight muscles
- Trouble falling or staying asleep
- Thoughts of hurting yourself: call or text 988 now

## What happens in your body when you are stressed?

When you sense a threat, your body launches what the Mayo Clinic calls the fight or flight response. A small area at the base of the brain sets off an alarm, and the adrenal glands release hormones including adrenaline, which raises your heart rate and blood pressure, and cortisol, which Mayo calls the main stress hormone. When the threat passes, those levels are meant to fall and your body settles back down. When stress is constant, the response stays switched on.

The Mayo Clinic explains that long term activation of this stress response can disrupt almost all of the body's processes. It links ongoing stress to anxiety, depression, trouble with focus, digestive problems, headaches, and poor sleep, along with heart disease, high blood pressure, and stroke. That is why caring for stress is not a luxury but part of caring for the body God gave you.

## How to manage stress with everyday habits

The best stress habits are simple, repeatable, and kind to your body. The Mayo Clinic advises starting with the basics of eating well, exercising regularly, and getting enough sleep, then adding relaxation practices, journaling, and time with friends. NIMH offers a similar list that includes keeping a journal, sticking to a sleep routine, avoiding excess caffeine, and challenging negative, unhelpful thoughts.

- Breathe slowly : Pause for a few slow, deep breaths when tension rises
- Move your body : Aim for brisk walks most days of the week
- Guard your sleep : Keep a steady bedtime and put screens away early
- Write it down : Journal worries, gratitude, and prayers
- Reach out : Talk with a trusted friend, pastor, or counselor

### Does deep breathing really help with stress?

Yes, slow breathing is a relaxation technique that health agencies describe as a generally safe way to calm the body. The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH) explains that techniques such as deep breathing, progressive relaxation, and guided imagery aim to produce the body's natural relaxation response, which includes slower breathing, lower blood pressure, and a feeling of calm. NCCIH says these techniques are generally safe and may work best when practiced regularly along with good nutrition, exercise, and social support. It cautions that they should never replace conventional medical care.

### How much exercise and sleep help with stress?

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that adults get 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity each week, such as brisk walking for 30 minutes on 5 days, plus muscle strengthening activity on at least 2 days. For sleep, the CDC advises 7 or more hours a night for adults ages 18 to 60, 7 to 9 hours for ages 61 to 64, and 7 to 8 hours for adults 65 and older. The Mayo Clinic adds a practical tip for better rest: stop using screens at least an hour before bed. Rest is one of God's oldest gifts, and we explore it more fully in our article on sleep.

Related: [The Gift of Rest: Why Sleep Is Part of Our Worship](https://shekinahsda.org/blog/the-gift-of-rest-why-sleep-is-part-of-our-worship/)

### Why does talking with someone help?

Talking with someone helps because stress feels lighter when it is shared, and many people are carrying more than they show. The American Psychological Association's Stress in America 2025 survey of 3,199 United States adults, conducted online by The Harris Poll in August 2025, found that 54 percent felt isolated often or some of the time. The same survey found that 69 percent said they needed more emotional support in the past year than they received. Both NIMH and the Mayo Clinic encourage reaching out to friends and family who help you cope in a positive way, and Mayo recommends professional counseling when you need help learning new coping skills.

## What does the Bible say about worry and stress?

The Bible teaches that worry is real, that God sees it, and that He invites us to hand it over to Him in prayer. Scripture does not shame worried people. Again and again it points them to a Father who knows what they need and a Savior who offers rest. Here are the passages that speak most directly to an anxious heart, all quoted from the King James Version.

### What does Philippians 4:6 to 7 mean?

Philippians 4:6 to 7 teaches that the answer to anxiety is to bring every need to God in prayer with thanksgiving, and that God responds with a peace beyond human understanding. In the older English of the King James Version, "be careful for nothing" means do not be anxious about anything, which is how many modern translations render it. Paul wrote these words from prison, not from a life free of hardship.

> "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus." Philippians 4:6 to 7, KJV

Notice that Paul does not promise every problem will disappear. He promises that God's peace will keep, or guard, your heart and mind. Thanksgiving matters too, because remembering what God has done steadies us for what we cannot yet see.

### What did Jesus say about worrying about tomorrow?

In Matthew 6:25 to 34, Jesus tells His followers not to be anxious about food, clothing, or tomorrow, because their heavenly Father knows what they need. The King James phrase "take no thought" is rendered "do not worry" in many modern translations, which shows that Jesus is speaking about anxious worry, not wise planning. He points to the birds of the air and the lilies of the field as proof of the Father's daily care.

> "But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you. Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." Matthew 6:33 to 34, KJV

Jesus also asks a gentle question in Matthew 6:27: "Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?" Worry cannot add a single thing to our lives. Living one day at a time, with God first, is His better way.

### How do I cast my cares on God?

To cast your cares on God means to deliberately hand Him each specific burden in prayer, trusting that He cares about you personally. Peter and David both use the picture of throwing a heavy load onto someone strong enough to carry it. In practice, that can be as simple as naming each worry out loud or on paper and saying, "Lord, I give this to You."

> "Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you." 1 Peter 5:7, KJV

> "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved." Psalm 55:22, KJV

Jesus makes the same offer in His own voice. In Matthew 11:28 to 30 He says, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light." Isaiah 26:3 adds the promise, "Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee."

| When you are thinking | Scripture to pray |
| --- | --- |
| I cannot handle all of this | 1 Peter 5:7 and Psalm 55:22 |
| What if tomorrow goes wrong? | Matthew 6:34 |
| I am exhausted inside and out | Matthew 11:28 to 30 |
| My mind will not settle | Isaiah 26:3 and Philippians 4:6 to 7 |

## How do the eight natural remedies help with stress?

Seventh-day Adventists often speak of eight natural remedies, and many of them line up with what health researchers recommend for stress. In her book The Ministry of Healing, Ellen G. White listed pure air, sunlight, abstemiousness (temperance), rest, exercise, proper diet, the use of water, and trust in divine power as "the true remedies." Fundamental Belief 22, Christian Behavior, teaches that because our bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit, we are to care for them intelligently with adequate exercise, rest, and the most healthful diet possible.

Here it helps to keep two things clearly separate. The medical facts in this article, such as the benefits of exercise, sleep, and relaxation practices, come from health agencies like the CDC, NIMH, NCCIH, and the Mayo Clinic. The spiritual application is our conviction as Seventh-day Adventists that caring for the body is an act of faithful stewardship, and that trust in God brings a peace no habit can produce on its own. A prayer walk in fresh air and sunlight is a lovely habit, but it is never a substitute for medical treatment.

The weekly Sabbath belongs here too, since the Seventh-day Adventist Church's explanation of Fundamental Belief 22 calls good sleep at the end of each day highly important and also points to resting at the end of the week on Sabbath. Setting aside work and worry from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset gives the whole family a rhythm of rest. God built that rhythm into creation itself.

## Carrying burdens in two places

Many immigrant families, including many Haitian families, carry concern for loved ones both here and back home. A phone call about a parent's health, news from Haiti, or the pressure to help relatives can add a heavy layer to everyday stress. Prayer is precious, and so is talking openly with a trusted friend, a pastor, or a counselor; there is no shame in asking for help. At Shekinah, we worship in Kreyòl and English, and you are welcome to pray and share in whichever language your heart speaks best.

## Questions people ask

### Is it a sin to worry?

The Bible does not treat the feeling of worry as a reason for shame, but it does invite us not to stay in worry and to hand it to God instead. Jesus' words in Matthew 6 are an invitation to trust the Father, spoken to people He loved, and Scripture responds to worried people with compassion rather than condemnation. If worry has become constant and overwhelming, that is a reason to seek support, not a reason for shame.

### Can prayer replace counseling or medication?

No, and Scripture never asks you to choose between them. NIMH explains that psychotherapy, also called talk therapy, and medication are the two main treatments for anxiety. A doctor or licensed counselor can be one of the ways God brings help to you, and seeking care is stewardship, not a lack of faith.

### Is it normal to feel stressed all the time?

Some stress is a normal part of life, but feeling stressed all the time is a signal to pay attention. NIMH says stress may be a concern if its symptoms seem to be always present, interfere with everyday life, or cause you to avoid doing things. If that describes you, talk with your doctor or a licensed mental health professional soon.

### What should I do if stress turns into thoughts of hurting myself?

If you are in immediate distress or thinking about hurting yourself, call or text the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988, or chat at 988lifeline.org, as the National Institute of Mental Health advises. If you are in danger right now, call 911. You matter to God and to the people around you, and reaching out is a brave and faithful step.

## Reflection questions

Which worry have you been carrying alone that you could name to God today, using the words of 1 Peter 5:7? What is one small habit from this article, such as a short walk, an earlier bedtime, or a few minutes of slow breathing, that you could begin this week? Who is one trusted person you could talk with honestly about what has been weighing on you?

## A word of encouragement

Jesus did not tell the crowds to stop being human; He told them they had a Father who knows what they need. God cares about your racing heart, your tired body, and your troubled mind. Take today's steps, bring today's worries to Him, and leave tomorrow in His hands.

## A prayer

Father, You know every worry I carry, even the ones I have not spoken out loud. I bring them to You now, because Your Word says You care for me. Calm my body, quiet my mind, and give me wisdom to care for the life You have given me. Lead me to the people and the help I need, and keep my heart in Your peace through Jesus Christ. Amen.
